title: The Conceptual Model
summary: The conceptual model is the bridge between what the customer said and what you are going to build. You classify every statement the customer makes into Requirements, Constraints, Assumptions and Risks (RCAR), decompose requirements into functional and non-functional halves, and then carry each item forward with a traceability ID so that every later design decision can be defended by pointing back to evidence. Nothing in the logical or physical design is allowed to exist without a conceptual-model parent.

components.name: RCAR Framework
components.what: RCAR is the classification scheme used to sort raw customer input into four buckets: Requirements (what the solution must do or must achieve), Constraints (boundaries imposed on the design that you cannot change), Assumptions (statements believed true but not yet validated), and Risks (conditions that could cause the design to fail its requirements). It sits at the very front of the design process, before any logical design work begins, and its output is the numbered evidence set (BRxx, Cxx, Axx, Rxx) that the rest of the design cites.
components.how: The input is unstructured discovery material: interview notes, workshop output, current-state assessment reports, capacity data. You read each statement and ask a sequence of tests. Does it describe an outcome the business needs? It is a requirement. Does it limit your freedom of choice (existing hardware, existing network, budget, regulation, skills)? It is a constraint. Is it stated as fact but unverified, or is it a projection about the future? It is an assumption, and it must be logged for validation. Would it, if true, threaten a requirement? It is a risk, and it needs a mitigation owner. Each item receives a stable identifier. Assumptions are the highest-value bucket because each one is a validation task you owe the customer, and an unvalidated assumption that later proves false is the single most common cause of a failed design.
components.why: Broadcom's design methodology insists on RCAR because architecture is a defensibility exercise as much as an engineering one. Without classification, designers conflate a preference with a requirement and end up defending a product choice rather than a business outcome. With classification, every design decision can be traced to a specific identifier, alternatives can be rejected on evidentiary grounds, and the customer can see exactly which of their statements drove which piece of the build. Use RCAR at the start of every engagement and revisit it whenever new discovery data arrives.
components.examTip: The exam gives you a customer statement and asks which RCAR category it belongs to. Learn the discriminators: 'we already have' or 'we must use' or 'we cannot change' equals constraint; 'we expect' or 'we believe' or 'traffic will grow' equals assumption; 'the business needs' equals requirement; 'if X happens we lose Y' equals risk. Existing infrastructure is always a constraint, never a requirement. A projection about future growth is always an assumption, never a requirement.

components.name: Functional and Non-Functional Requirements
components.what: A functional requirement states what the solution must do: a capability, a behaviour, a feature that either exists or does not. A non-functional requirement states how well the solution must do it: the quality level, expressed as a measurable target such as availability percentage, latency ceiling, recovery time objective, or throughput floor. Both live inside the Requirements bucket of RCAR, and together they define the acceptance criteria for the design.
components.how: Decomposition is the mechanism. A single business requirement such as 'support the developer platform' is too coarse to design against, so you split it. The functional side yields items like 'provide self-service VM provisioning' and 'provide Kubernetes cluster provisioning'. The non-functional side yields items like 'provision within 10 minutes at the 95th percentile' and 'sustain 99.9 percent platform availability'. The functional items drive which components you select; the non-functional items drive how you configure, size and make them resilient. A non-functional requirement without a number is not yet a requirement, it is an aspiration, and part of the architect's job is to force the number out of the customer.
components.why: Broadcom separates the two because they consume different design levers. You satisfy functional requirements by choosing components; you satisfy non-functional requirements by choosing topology, redundancy, sizing and policy. If you do not separate them you will build something that technically has all the features and still fails acceptance because nobody quantified 'fast' or 'highly available'. The non-functional set is also what the AMPRS lens evaluates, so a design with weak non-functional requirements cannot be assessed for trade-offs.
components.examTip: Non-functional equals quality level equals a measurable target. If the answer option mentions a percentage, a time limit, a latency figure or a throughput figure, it is non-functional. If it names a capability or feature, it is functional. Expect a question that hands you a mixed list and asks you to sort it.

components.name: AMPRS Quality Lens
components.what: AMPRS stands for Availability, Manageability, Performance, Recoverability and Security. In the conceptual model it functions as a checklist applied to the non-functional requirement set, ensuring that all five quality dimensions have been elicited rather than just the one or two the customer happened to mention. It reappears in Module 8 as the evaluation lens for design decisions.
components.how: You walk each requirement through the five dimensions and record the target and the evidence. Availability asks what interruption is tolerable. Manageability asks who operates it and with what tooling and skills. Performance asks what throughput, latency and headroom are needed. Recoverability asks what RTO and RPO apply and what must be restorable. Security asks what identity, encryption, segmentation and compliance regime governs it. Gaps found here become either new requirements or new assumptions to validate. Later, when you make a design decision, you re-run the same five dimensions to state the trade-off the decision creates, because improving one dimension almost always costs another.
components.why: Broadcom uses AMPRS because unstated quality expectations are where designs die. A customer who never mentioned recoverability still expects to be able to restore, and a customer who never mentioned manageability still has a two-person operations team. Forcing all five dimensions early makes those expectations explicit while they are still cheap to satisfy. Applying AMPRS to decisions rather than only to requirements is what turns a list of choices into an architecture with declared trade-offs.
components.examTip: Know the five words cold and in order. The exam tests both the expansion of the acronym and the ability to name which dimension a given trade-off affects. Remember that manageability includes operational skill and tooling burden, not just management components, and that improving availability commonly costs manageability and cost.

components.name: VCF Planning and Preparation Workbook
components.what: The Planning and Preparation Workbook is the Broadcom-published spreadsheet that enumerates every prerequisite and input value a VCF deployment needs: DNS and NTP records, VLAN IDs and subnets, MTU values, certificate details, licence keys, host inventory, IP pools and appliance sizing selections. It is the formal handoff artefact between the design and the deployment, and it is the document the VCF Installer draws from.
components.how: You complete the workbook as the logical design converges, filling each row from a traceable design decision rather than from guesswork. The workbook then drives the VCF Installer inputs, which in VCF 9 is a guided UI flow that can also import JSON configuration templates. Because the Installer performs hard validations, notably the TEP-to-TEP MTU check, a workbook value that disagrees with the physical network will surface as a deployment blocker rather than a runtime surprise. The workbook is also the checklist for the external services the platform depends on: forward and reverse DNS for every appliance FQDN, NTP reachability, and routable subnets per traffic type.
components.why: Broadcom ships the workbook because the overwhelming majority of failed VCF deployments fail on prerequisites rather than on architecture. Centralising the inputs makes gaps visible before hardware is racked and gives the customer a single artefact to action across their DNS, network and security teams. For an architect it also serves as evidence that the logical design was completed to physical-input fidelity.
components.examTip: Expect a question on what the workbook is for and what belongs in it. It captures deployment inputs and prerequisites, not design rationale. In VCF 9 the Cloud Builder spreadsheet workflow has been replaced by the guided VCF Installer, but the planning workbook remains the design-to-deploy artefact.

components.name: Traceability
components.what: Traceability is the discipline of tagging every design decision with the identifiers of the RCAR items it satisfies, so that the design forms a directed graph from business evidence through logical decision to physical configuration. In practice it is the list of IDs such as BR05, C02, A02 attached to each design decision record.
components.how: Each requirement, constraint, assumption and risk gets an ID when it is captured. Each design decision record then names the IDs it addresses, states the recommendation, the rationale, the rejected alternatives and the AMPRS impact. Reading forward from an ID tells you which decisions depend on it, which is what makes change control tractable: if assumption A02 is invalidated during validation, you can immediately enumerate every decision that must be revisited. Reading backwards from a decision tells you why it exists, which is what makes design review possible without the original author in the room.
components.why: Broadcom's design methodology treats an untraceable decision as an undefendable one. Traceability is also the mechanism that keeps scope honest, because a decision with no upstream ID is either gold-plating or a missing requirement. On a real engagement it is the difference between a design document and a product configuration guide.
components.examTip: The exam frames this as 'what must drive every logical design decision' and the answer is the conceptual model, not a product preference, not the instructor's example, not cost. Also expect to be asked what makes a decision defendable: the traceability links plus the rejected alternatives.

keyFacts: RCAR equals Requirements, Constraints, Assumptions, Risks.
Every logical design decision must be driven by the conceptual model, never by product preference.
Functional requirement equals what the solution does; non-functional requirement equals the quality level, expressed as a measurable target.
Existing infrastructure that must be reused is always a constraint. In the case study, C02 is the existing network.
A forward-looking projection such as 'development workload will triple' is always an assumption and must be logged for validation.
AMPRS equals Availability, Manageability, Performance, Recoverability, Security.
Conflicting statements, such as a 30-day deadline against a 90-day dependency, are surfaced in the conceptual model as a risk or a conflict to resolve, not silently reconciled.
Consumed capacity figures alone (TB used, allocated memory) are insufficient for sizing; you need performance and growth evidence too.
The Planning and Preparation Workbook carries deployment inputs and prerequisites; the design decision records carry rationale.
Every design decision record should state recommendation, rationale, rejected alternative, AMPRS impact and traceability IDs.
attentionItems: Confusing a constraint with a requirement. 'We must reuse the existing L3 spine-leaf fabric' is a constraint on your freedom, not a business outcome.
Treating a growth projection as a requirement. Tripling development workload is an assumption until the customer validates the forecast; the requirement is to support the resulting capacity.
Writing non-functional requirements without numbers. 'Highly available' is not a requirement; '99.9 percent monthly availability' is.
Extrapolating from allocated or consumed values. Allocated memory reflects what someone requested, not what the workload uses; consumed TB says nothing about IOPS, growth rate or working-set size.
Resolving a schedule conflict by assuming the optimistic case. If a hard deadline conflicts with a dependency lead time, that is a risk with an owner, not an accounting adjustment.
Skipping assumption validation because the customer sounded confident. Unvalidated assumptions are the most common root cause of design failure.
Believing a hardware compatibility listing settles a design question. Compatibility proves supportability, not fitness for the workload's performance and capacity profile.

vcf91Updates.title: VCF Installer supersedes the Cloud Builder spreadsheet workflow
vcf91Updates.description: The deployment entry point is now a guided flow in the VCF Operations user interface with support for importing JSON configuration templates, replacing the Cloud Builder spreadsheet upload. Cloud Builder is fully retired.
vcf91Updates.impact: The Planning and Preparation Workbook is still the artefact where you assemble and validate deployment inputs, but the handoff into deployment is now a guided UI or a JSON template rather than a spreadsheet import. Conceptual-model outputs should be captured in a form that maps cleanly onto the Installer's input schema.

title: Networking
summary: VCF 9 networking is two layers that must be designed together: a routed physical underlay, normally a Layer 3 spine-leaf fabric with redundant top-of-rack switches, and a Geneve-encapsulated NSX overlay that rides on top of it via host tunnel endpoints on a vSphere Distributed Switch. The design work is deciding single-rack versus multi-rack cluster models, proving end-to-end MTU for the overlay path, and sizing bandwidth with real headroom rather than nameplate link speed. In the case study the existing fabric is a constraint (C02), so the design retains the L3 spine-leaf underlay and validates that it can carry the overlay.

components.name: Layer 3 Spine-Leaf Underlay
components.what: The physical network fabric that carries all VCF traffic. Each rack has a redundant pair of top-of-rack (leaf) switches, every ESX host dual-attaches to both leaves with 802.1Q trunks, and the leaves uplink to spine switches. In a Layer 3 model the routing boundary sits at the top of rack, so each rack owns its own subnets and the spine layer routes between racks.
components.how: VLANs are provisioned per traffic type and trunked to every host uplink: ESX host management, VM management, vSphere vMotion, vSAN, NSX host overlay (host TEP), NSX Edge overlay (edge TEP) and NSX Edge uplinks. Note that management is two VLANs, not one: a VLAN for host management and a separate VLAN for the VM management network where the VCF appliances run. In a Layer 3 multi-rack model each of these functions is rack-local with a separate subnet per rack and a highly available first-hop gateway at the leaves (HSRP, VRRP or anycast), and the networks must be routable across racks. BGP is the usual routing protocol, and it is also how NSX Edge nodes peer with the fabric to advertise overlay networks northbound. Broadcom's reference physical design recommends two ToR switches per rack and 25 GbE host uplinks with 10 GbE as the floor.
components.why: A routed fabric scales linearly, keeps failure and broadcast domains small, and removes the large stretched Layer 2 domains that make traditional data centre networks fragile. Broadcom aligns VCF on spine-leaf because the overlay supplies logical Layer 2 adjacency where workloads need it, so the physical fabric no longer has to. Choose Layer 3 multi-rack when racks are independent failure and power domains and you want rack-level resilience plus horizontal scale; choose a single-rack model when the cluster fits in one rack and you would rather not carry the extra routing and IP-management overhead.
components.examTip: Know that in a Layer 3 multi-rack cluster you use a separate host TEP transport VLAN and subnet per rack, with a highly available gateway at the top of rack. If a question hands you an existing L3 spine-leaf fabric as a constraint, the correct move is to retain it and validate overlay support, not to redesign the fabric.

components.name: VXLAN and Geneve Overlay
components.what: The overlay is the logical network layer that encapsulates workload Ethernet frames inside UDP packets so they can be carried across a routed underlay. NSX in VCF uses Geneve encapsulation (the successor to VXLAN, and the term VXLAN is still used generically for tunnelled overlays and specifically for the new EVPN-VXLAN fabric interoperability in 9.1). Encapsulation and decapsulation happen at tunnel endpoints (TEPs) on each transport node.
components.how: Each ESX host prepared as an NSX transport node gets one or more TEP VMkernel interfaces on the TEP VLAN. When a VM sends a frame, the host looks up the destination's TEP, wraps the frame in a Geneve header plus outer UDP/IP headers, and sends it to the remote TEP across the underlay; the remote host strips the headers and delivers the original frame. Because the outer headers add roughly 100 bytes, the underlay MTU must exceed the guest MTU. The hard floor for the TEP path is 1600 bytes, Broadcom recommends at least 1700 to absorb Geneve header growth, and 9000 (jumbo) is the optimal setting where the underlay supports it. All transport nodes for a domain share a single overlay transport zone so that every host and Edge node can reach every segment and VPC.
components.why: The overlay decouples workload addressing and adjacency from the physical fabric, which is what makes self-service networking, multi-tenancy and workload mobility possible without touching switch configuration. Broadcom made the overlay mandatory for full VCF capability, notably VPC networking and Supervisor, because tenant-driven network creation cannot depend on a network team provisioning VLANs.
components.examTip: The overlay's non-negotiable dependency is consistent MTU end to end. 1600 is the minimum the installer validates, 1700 is the recommendation, 9000 is optimal. Also remember that a single overlay transport zone per NSX instance is the design requirement.

components.name: NSX
components.what: NSX is the software-defined networking and security layer of VCF. It comprises an NSX Manager cluster (management and control plane), the distributed data plane implemented in every prepared ESX host, and NSX Edge nodes that provide centralised services and north-south routing. In VCF it is deployed and lifecycle-managed as part of a domain rather than installed independently.
components.how: Hosts are prepared as transport nodes using transport node profiles applied at cluster level, which is why transport node configuration is a cluster-scoped decision. NSX then provides logical segments, distributed routing, the distributed firewall, VPCs, load balancing and gateway services. The management domain gets an NSX Manager cluster; the first workload domain gets its own NSX Manager cluster deployed into the management domain, and additional workload domains can either share an existing NSX Manager cluster or receive a new one, which is a deliberate lifecycle and isolation decision. NSX is prepared directly on a VDS of version 8.0 or later; there is no legacy N-VDS in VCF 9.
components.why: Broadcom centralises networking and micro-segmentation in NSX so that security policy follows the workload rather than the wire, and so that consumption layers such as Supervisor and VCF Automation have an API-driven network to carve up. Sharing an NSX Manager cluster reduces appliance count and cost; separating it gives independent lifecycle and a smaller blast radius, which is the usual reason to accept the extra footprint.
components.examTip: Know the sharing rule for NSX Manager across workload domains: share with an existing domain or the management domain, or deploy a new cluster. The trade-off is footprint and cost against lifecycle independence and failure isolation.

components.name: vSphere Distributed Switch (VDS)
components.what: The VDS is the virtual switch object defined at the vCenter level and pushed to every host in the cluster, providing consistent port groups, uplink teaming, VLAN tagging and MTU configuration across the whole cluster. In VCF 9 it must be version 8.0 or later and it is the substrate NSX prepares for overlay traffic.
components.how: VCF creates and manages the VDS for each cluster, mapping physical NICs to uplinks and creating distributed port groups for the VLAN-backed traffic types. Because configuration is centralised in vCenter and applied uniformly, host-level configuration drift is eliminated. The MTU set on the VDS and its port groups must match the physical fabric and the NSX TEP setting; a VDS at 9000 over a fabric at 1500 produces the classic failure signature where small pings succeed but vSAN, vMotion and NSX tunnels break. A design decision that frequently appears is whether to use a single VDS carrying all traffic types or separate VDS instances to segregate storage traffic from workload traffic.
components.why: Broadcom standardises on the VDS because consistency is a manageability and availability property: identical switch configuration on every host is what lets DRS, HA, vMotion and NSX behave predictably. Separate VDS instances buy physical isolation for storage traffic at the cost of more uplinks and more configuration surface; a single VDS is simpler to operate and is normally sufficient when uplink bandwidth is adequate.
components.examTip: Remember that the VDS is one of several places MTU must agree, and that all of them must agree: physical switches and routers, VDS and port groups, VMkernel adapters, and the NSX global TEP setting.

components.name: VMkernel Networks
components.what: VMkernel adapters are the host's own IP interfaces, each enabled for one or more system traffic services: management, vMotion, vSAN, vSAN witness, NSX host overlay (TEP), NFS and others. They are the endpoints for all infrastructure traffic, as distinct from workload traffic which terminates on VM vNICs.
components.how: Each VMkernel adapter is placed on a distributed port group carrying the appropriate VLAN and inherits or sets an MTU. In a Layer 3 multi-rack model each service gets a rack-local subnet, so hosts in different racks have different VMkernel addresses for the same service and rely on the fabric to route between them. Verification is done from the host with a do-not-fragment ping sized to the payload, for example vmkping with the don't-fragment flag and a payload of 8972 bytes to prove a 9000-byte path, and it must be run between hosts in different racks and across different leaf pairs, because the failure is almost always at the Layer 3 boundary rather than within a rack.
components.why: Separating infrastructure traffic onto dedicated VMkernel interfaces and VLANs is what allows independent MTU, quality of service and failure isolation per traffic type. Broadcom requires this separation because vSAN and overlay traffic have jumbo-frame and latency characteristics that management traffic does not, and mixing them without separation makes performance problems undiagnosable.
components.examTip: Expect a validation question. The correct answer for proving overlay readiness is a do-not-fragment ping between TEPs at the target frame size, run across racks, not a configuration review. Configured does not equal working.

keyFacts: The case study existing network is constraint C02; the design retains the L3 spine-leaf underlay rather than replacing it.
Overlay TEP path MTU: 1600 bytes is the hard minimum the installer validates, 1700 is the Broadcom recommendation, 9000 is optimal for throughput.
MTU must agree across physical switches and routers, the VDS and its port groups, the VMkernel adapters, and the NSX global TEP setting.
Measured peak of 9 Gbps on 10 Gb links means roughly 90 percent utilisation, which leaves no headroom for burst, failover or growth.
Broadcom's physical network recommendation is two ToR switches per rack and 25 GbE host uplinks with 10 GbE as the minimum.
A Layer 3 multi-rack cluster uses a separate host TEP VLAN and subnet per rack, with a highly available first-hop gateway at the top of rack.
Management requires two VLANs: ESX host management and a separate VM management network for the VCF appliances.
VDS must be version 8.0 or later; NSX is prepared directly on the VDS and there is no N-VDS in VCF 9.
A single overlay transport zone per NSX instance serves all overlay traffic for the domains sharing that NSX Manager.
Validate MTU with a do-not-fragment vmkping across racks, not just within a rack.
attentionItems: Assuming nameplate link speed equals usable bandwidth. A 9 Gbps peak on a 10 Gb link is a headroom problem, not a healthy result.
Setting jumbo frames on the VDS and host uplinks while leaving the physical fabric or an intermediate Layer 3 hop at 1500. Small pings still work, which hides the fault until load arrives.
Forgetting the router or spine between racks when setting MTU. Traffic works inside a rack and fails across racks.
Using the MTU validation skip flag to get past an installer failure. That defers the failure into production NSX as intermittent packet loss, which is far harder to diagnose.
Confusing VXLAN and Geneve. NSX in VCF encapsulates with Geneve; VXLAN is the generic term and, in 9.1, the specific EVPN-VXLAN fabric interoperability feature.
Choosing multi-rack for its own sake. Multi-rack only buys resilience if the racks are genuinely independent power, cooling and network failure domains.
Treating overlay adoption as optional. VPC networking and the full Supervisor and VCF Automation capability set depend on it.

designDecisions.question: Should the VCF 9 management domain be deployed on the newly acquired hardware, or should existing hardware be converged or reused?
designDecisions.recommendation: Deploy a new VCF 9 management domain on the new hardware.
designDecisions.rationale: New hardware gives a clean, fully supported foundation that meets VCF 9 requirements without carrying forward the constraints, firmware levels and lifecycle state of the existing estate. It also decouples the build from the production environment, so the management domain can be stood up and validated while existing workloads continue to run, which is what makes a staged migration possible.
designDecisions.alternative: Converging or upgrading existing hardware in place was rejected because it couples the new platform's timeline to the old estate's maintenance windows, inherits unvalidated firmware and compatibility state, and removes the ability to fall back to the current environment during migration.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Availability improves because the build has no impact on running production. Manageability improves through a single consistent hardware and software baseline. Recoverability improves because the existing environment remains as a fallback throughout the migration. Cost increases, and the estate is temporarily dual-running.

designDecisions.question: Should the existing Layer 3 spine-leaf underlay be retained for VCF 9, or should the fabric be redesigned?
designDecisions.recommendation: Retain the existing Layer 3 spine-leaf underlay and validate that it supports the NSX overlay end to end.
designDecisions.rationale: The existing fabric is a constraint (C02) and it is already the topology Broadcom recommends for VCF. The requirement is therefore not to redesign it but to prove it: confirm MTU of at least 1600 and preferably 1700 or 9000 across every hop including the spine and any intermediate Layer 3 device, confirm per-rack VLANs and subnets with highly available gateways, and confirm BGP peering capability for NSX Edge uplinks.
designDecisions.alternative: A fabric redesign or a Layer 2 stretched design was rejected because C02 constrains the network, a redesign adds cost, risk and schedule with no requirement driving it, and large stretched Layer 2 domains are the topology VCF's overlay exists to avoid.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Manageability and cost benefit from reusing a known fabric and skill set. Performance and availability are conditional on the validation passing, which is why confidence is medium-high rather than high: an unvalidated MTU path is an open risk. Security is unchanged.

designDecisions.question: Should clusters use a multi-rack Layer 3 cluster model or a single-rack cluster model?
designDecisions.recommendation: Use the multi-rack Layer 3 cluster model where the racks are validated as independent power, cooling and network failure domains; otherwise use the single-rack model.
designDecisions.rationale: Multi-rack distributes a cluster's hosts across racks so that the loss of a rack does not take the cluster down, and it allows horizontal growth beyond a single rack's capacity. Both benefits depend entirely on rack independence, which is a facilities fact that must be validated rather than assumed.
designDecisions.alternative: A single-rack model was not rejected outright; it remains correct where the cluster fits in one rack, where rack independence cannot be demonstrated, or where the additional per-rack VLAN, subnet and gateway management is not justified.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Availability improves materially if the racks are truly independent, and not at all if they share a power feed or upstream switch. Manageability degrades because of per-rack subnets, TEP VLANs and gateway redundancy. Performance is broadly neutral, though inter-rack traffic now traverses the spine.

vcf91Updates.title: Distributed EVPN-VXLAN interoperability with physical switch fabrics
vcf91Updates.description: VCF 9.1 introduces Distributed Transit Gateway with EVPN-VXLAN connectivity, allowing workloads to integrate directly with EVPN-VXLAN fabrics using BGP EVPN and VXLAN without centralised gateway appliances in the traffic path. The BGP EVPN control-plane relationship is held by the VCF Route Controller peering with the fabric's EVPN border gateways, and forwarding is distributed closer to the workload. Broadcom announced validated interoperability with Arista's Universal Cloud Network as the first ecosystem integration.
vcf91Updates.impact: Where the customer's fabric already runs EVPN-VXLAN, this removes the centralised Edge appliance from the north-south data path, which changes Edge cluster sizing and placement decisions and improves scale and performance. It does not change the MTU validation obligation or the per-rack VLAN design in a Layer 3 multi-rack model, and it makes the state of the customer's fabric control plane a design input worth discovering explicitly.

title: Storage
summary: Storage design in VCF 9 centres on vSAN as the principal storage model, with the Express Storage Architecture (ESA) as the modern choice and the Original Storage Architecture (OSA) retained mainly for legacy hardware. Policy is expressed per workload through Storage Policy Based Management (SPBM), with failures to tolerate (FTT) and the data placement scheme (mirroring versus erasure coding) as the primary levers. In the case study the 8 Gbps Fibre Channel SAN is end of life, which makes the retirement of external block storage a driver rather than an option.

components.name: vSAN Express Storage Architecture (ESA)
components.what: ESA is the current vSAN data path and on-disk format, introduced in vSAN 8 and the default for VCF 9. It is designed for all-NVMe ReadyNode hardware and uses a single-tier device model, with no separate cache and capacity tiers, so every device contributes both performance and capacity.
components.how: ESA's log-structured file system and log-structured object manager ingest writes into a performance leg and then write full stripes with parity, which is why erasure coding no longer carries the write-amplification penalty it did in OSA. Compression happens once at the top of the stack before data is transmitted, so it saves network as well as capacity. RAID-5 in ESA adapts its scheme to cluster size rather than being fixed at 3+1: below six hosts it uses a 2+1 stripe (1.5x overhead) and at six or more hosts it uses 4+1 (1.25x overhead), readjusting automatically roughly 24 hours after a cluster size change. RAID-6 uses 4+2 for a 1.5x overhead. Because erasure coding performs at mirroring-like levels, Broadcom's guidance is to reserve RAID-1 mirroring for site resilience in stretched clusters and host resilience in two-node clusters.
components.why: Broadcom built ESA to remove the historical trade-off between performance and space efficiency: architects previously chose RAID-1 for performance and paid double or triple capacity, or chose erasure coding and paid a write penalty. Removing that trade-off makes space-efficient resilience the default and materially lowers the cost per usable terabyte on all-flash hardware. Choose ESA for any new build on all-NVMe ReadyNodes, which is the normal case in VCF 9.
components.examTip: Know that ESA is single-tier all-NVMe with no cache and capacity tier split, that it makes erasure coding performant enough to be the default, and that its RAID-5 scheme adapts to host count (2+1 below six hosts, 4+1 at six or more). Recommended minimums are four hosts for FTT=1 RAID-5 and seven hosts for FTT=2 RAID-6, because you want a spare fault domain.

components.name: vSAN Original Storage Architecture (OSA)
components.what: OSA is the classic vSAN architecture, using disk groups in which one cache device fronts several capacity devices. It remains supported in VCF 9 and 9.1 but is the legacy choice, appropriate where hardware is hybrid or SAS/SATA-based rather than all-NVMe.
components.how: Writes land in the cache tier and are destaged to capacity, so cache device sizing and failure domain are first-order design concerns: losing a cache device takes its whole disk group offline. RAID-5 in OSA is a fixed 3+1 scheme requiring at least four hosts, giving 1.33x overhead, and erasure coding carries a real write amplification penalty, which is why OSA designs commonly chose RAID-1 mirroring for performance-sensitive workloads and accepted 2x or 3x capacity overhead. The newer efficiency features in 9.1, notably global deduplication and Auto-RAID, are ESA-only.
components.why: Broadcom keeps OSA available so that existing hardware and hybrid configurations are not stranded, but new capability lands in ESA. For an architect the practical rule is that OSA is a constraint-driven choice: you pick it because the hardware forces you to, not because the design prefers it.
components.examTip: The examinable contrast is: OSA has cache plus capacity disk groups, fixed 3+1 RAID-5, and a genuine erasure coding write penalty; ESA is single-tier all-NVMe, adaptive RAID-5, and no meaningful erasure coding penalty. Auto-RAID and global dedup are ESA-only.

components.name: Storage Policy Based Management (SPBM)
components.what: SPBM is the vSphere framework that expresses storage requirements as policies attached to virtual machines and individual virtual disks, rather than as properties of a datastore. It is the single unified control plane across vSAN, vVols, NFS, array-based storage and I/O filters.
components.how: Storage providers advertise their capabilities to vCenter; you build a policy by selecting the capabilities and values a workload needs; you attach the policy at VM create, clone or migrate time. SPBM then places the object on a compatible datastore, instantiates the requested data services, and continuously reports compliance, flagging drift when the underlying storage no longer satisfies the policy. On vSAN the policy directly determines object layout: failures to tolerate, the RAID scheme, stripe width, object space reservation and encryption. Because policy is per object, two VMs on the same vSAN datastore can have completely different resilience and space-efficiency characteristics, and a single VM can have different policies on different disks.
components.why: Broadcom designed SPBM so that storage service levels follow the workload instead of being baked into LUN or datastore boundaries. That is what removes the traditional practice of pre-provisioning tiers of datastores and hoping workloads land in the right one, and it is what lets a consumption layer such as Supervisor or VCF Automation offer storage classes to tenants declaratively.
components.examTip: SPBM equals per-workload storage policy, enforced at placement and monitored for compliance thereafter. It is object-level, not datastore-level, and it is the mechanism by which FTT and RAID scheme are applied.

components.name: Storage Policy and Failures To Tolerate (FTT)
components.what: A vSAN storage policy is the concrete set of rules SPBM applies to an object. Failures to tolerate (FTT) is its central rule: the number of concurrent host or device failures the object's data must survive. The companion rule is the data placement method, either RAID-1 mirroring or RAID-5/RAID-6 erasure coding.
components.how: FTT and placement together determine capacity overhead and host count. FTT=1 with mirroring keeps a second full copy, so 100 GB consumes 200 GB. FTT=1 with RAID-5 in ESA consumes 150 GB at 2+1 or 125 GB at 4+1. FTT=2 with mirroring consumes 300 GB; FTT=2 with RAID-6 consumes 150 GB. FTT=3 mirroring consumes 400 GB. Each combination also implies a minimum host count and, for real designs, a recommended count one higher so that the cluster can rebuild to full resilience during a failure or maintenance window: four hosts recommended for FTT=1 RAID-5 and seven for FTT=2 RAID-6 in ESA. In 9.1, Auto-RAID can take this decision over, selecting the layout from cluster topology and re-evaluating as the cluster changes.
components.why: Broadcom exposes FTT as the policy lever because resilience is a per-workload business decision, not a platform-wide one. A development workload may be entirely content with FTT=1 erasure coding, while a production database earns FTT=2. Expressing that as policy rather than as separate storage silos is what keeps a single cluster serving mixed service levels.
components.examTip: FTT means failures to tolerate. Memorise the overhead table and the host-count minimums, and remember the design rule of running at least one host above the policy minimum so resilience can be restored during maintenance.

components.name: vSAN ReadyNode and the Compatibility Guide
components.what: A vSAN ReadyNode is a server configuration pre-validated by Broadcom and the hardware vendor for vSAN, specifying models, device classes, controllers and firmware. The Broadcom Compatibility Guide (the hardware compatibility list) is the authoritative record of what is supported. ESA additionally requires ESA-certified ReadyNodes.
components.how: You select a ReadyNode profile that matches the workload's CPU, memory, capacity and device-class requirements, then verify every component including NIC, controller and firmware against the compatibility guide. The guide answers whether a configuration is supportable; it does not answer whether it is adequate. Sizing adequacy comes from measured evidence: IOPS and latency profiles, working-set size, growth rate and required headroom. In the case study, 200 TB used and peak requirements around 60,000 and 240,000 IOPS are the numbers that drive device count and class, while the compatibility guide only bounds which hardware you may use to deliver them.
components.why: Broadcom pre-validates ReadyNodes because vSAN's behaviour depends intimately on device and controller characteristics, and unvalidated combinations produce performance and reliability problems that look like software faults. The distinction between supportable and adequate exists because architects routinely mistake a compatibility tick for a design justification.
components.examTip: The exam tests exactly one idea here: the compatibility guide proves compatibility and supportability, not fitness for purpose. Sizing still requires performance and growth evidence. ESA requires ESA-certified all-NVMe ReadyNodes.

keyFacts: The existing 8 Gbps Fibre Channel SAN is end of life, which makes retiring external block storage a driver in the case study.
Roughly 200 TB is currently consumed, with peak requirements around 60,000 and 240,000 IOPS; consumed capacity alone is not a sizing basis.
vSAN ESA is single-tier all-NVMe with no cache and capacity tier split; OSA uses disk groups with a cache device fronting capacity devices.
ESA erasure coding performs at mirroring-like levels, so RAID-5/6 is the default and RAID-1 is reserved for stretched-cluster site resilience and two-node host resilience.
ESA RAID-5 adapts to cluster size: 2+1 (1.5x overhead) below six hosts, 4+1 (1.25x overhead) at six or more, readjusting about 24 hours after a size change.
OSA RAID-5 is a fixed 3+1 scheme needing at least four hosts, giving 1.33x overhead, with a real write amplification penalty.
Capacity overheads: FTT=1 mirroring 2x, FTT=2 mirroring 3x, FTT=3 mirroring 4x, FTT=2 RAID-6 1.5x.
Recommended host counts in ESA: four hosts for FTT=1 RAID-5, seven hosts for FTT=2 RAID-6, so a spare fault domain exists.
SPBM applies policy per virtual machine and per virtual disk, places objects on compatible storage, and reports compliance continuously.
The Broadcom Compatibility Guide proves supportability, not fitness; ESA requires ESA-certified ReadyNodes.
attentionItems: Sizing from consumed terabytes alone. You also need IOPS, latency targets, working-set size, growth rate and the capacity overhead of the chosen FTT and RAID scheme.
Carrying OSA-era instincts into ESA. Defaulting to RAID-1 for performance wastes capacity in ESA, where erasure coding no longer carries the penalty.
Assuming RAID-5 in ESA is 3+1. That is OSA. ESA adapts between 2+1 and 4+1 based on host count.
Building a cluster at exactly the policy minimum host count. There is then no spare fault domain, so resilience cannot be restored during a failure or maintenance.
Treating a compatibility guide entry as sizing evidence.
Expecting Auto-RAID or global deduplication on OSA. Both are ESA-only capabilities.
Forgetting that vSAN traffic has its own VMkernel interface, VLAN and MTU requirements, so a storage decision is also a network decision.

designDecisions.question: Which storage model should the VCF 9 management domain use?
designDecisions.recommendation: Use vSAN ESA for the management domain.
designDecisions.rationale: vSAN ESA is the principal storage model for VCF 9 and is delivered on the new all-NVMe ReadyNode hardware, giving the management domain policy-driven resilience with space-efficient erasure coding and no dependency on the end-of-life Fibre Channel SAN. It also keeps the management domain self-contained, so the platform's own control plane does not depend on external storage availability.
designDecisions.alternative: Retaining the existing 8 Gbps Fibre Channel SAN was rejected because it is end of life and would tie the new platform's lifecycle and availability to hardware scheduled for retirement. vSAN OSA was rejected because the new hardware is all-NVMe, so OSA would forgo ESA's performance and space efficiency for no benefit.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Availability and recoverability improve by removing the external SAN as a dependency of the management plane. Performance improves through all-NVMe single-tier ESA. Manageability improves because storage becomes policy-driven and lifecycle-managed with the platform. Security is unchanged, with encryption available through policy.
relatedComponents: vSAN ReadyNode and the Compatibility Guide

designDecisions.question: Which storage model should the development workload domain use?
designDecisions.recommendation: Use vSAN ESA for the development workload domain, with per-workload SPBM policies.
designDecisions.rationale: ESA gives the development domain a scale-out, policy-driven datastore that can serve differentiated service levels from a single cluster, so development, test and shared services can each carry an appropriate FTT and placement scheme. It also aligns the workload domain with the management domain on a single storage architecture, which keeps operational practice and lifecycle uniform, and it retires the dependency on the end-of-life SAN.
designDecisions.alternative: Continuing to consume the existing Fibre Channel SAN was rejected on end-of-life and 8 Gbps bandwidth grounds. A separate external array was rejected because it reintroduces a second storage lifecycle, a second skill set and a second failure domain with no requirement driving it.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Performance and scalability improve on all-NVMe ESA with headroom to grow by adding hosts. Manageability improves through one storage architecture across domains and per-workload policy instead of datastore tiers. Availability depends on the FTT policy chosen, which is deliberately deferred to DD-705. Cost is sensitive to that FTT choice because capacity overhead varies from 1.25x to 3x.
relatedComponents: Storage Policy and Failures To Tolerate (FTT)

vcf91Updates.title: Extended vSAN deduplication and enhanced compression
vcf91Updates.description: VCF 9.1 broadens inline data reduction across cluster types and workload profiles, moves deduplication to operate globally at the cluster level, adds deduplication support alongside data-at-rest encryption, and improves compression efficiency. Broadcom cites a substantial reduction in block storage total cost of ownership from the change.
vcf91Updates.impact: Usable-capacity calculations improve, so raw capacity sizing for a given logical requirement can come down. Because data reduction now coexists with encryption, a security requirement for data-at-rest encryption no longer costs you space efficiency. These are ESA capabilities, which strengthens the case for ESA over OSA in DD-501 and DD-502.

vcf91Updates.title: Auto-RAID system-managed resilience
vcf91Updates.description: Auto-RAID lets vSAN ESA select the data placement scheme automatically from cluster topology, preferring space-efficient erasure coding: FTT=1 RAID-5 (2+1) at three to five hosts and FTT=2 RAID-6 (4+2) at six or more, both at 1.5x overhead. It continuously re-evaluates as the cluster changes and reserves mirroring for stretched-cluster site resilience and two-node host resilience. Auto-RAID is ESA-only.
vcf91Updates.impact: The FTT and placement design decision shifts from a static policy choice to a decision about whether to delegate placement to the platform. Where Auto-RAID is adopted, DD-705 becomes a decision to accept system-managed resilience rather than a manual mirroring-versus-erasure-coding trade-off, and the 4+1 RAID-5 scheme is no longer used.

vcf91Updates.title: NVMe memory tiering as a capacity lever
vcf91Updates.description: ESX 9.1 tiers active pages in DRAM and cold pages onto local NVMe devices, expanding effective memory capacity without adding DRAM. In 9.1 it no longer requires a host reboot to enable or change device selection, it supports all VM types including low-latency, security and monster VMs, and it can mirror the tiering device with software RAID-1 so that a device failure does not stop tiering.
vcf91Updates.impact: Memory pressure evidence, such as high memory utilisation with ballooning, can now be addressed partly through tiering rather than exclusively through DRAM purchase or host count, which changes host sizing and cost models. It also makes local NVMe device selection and mirroring a storage design consideration rather than purely a compute one.

vcf91Updates.title: vVols deprecation
vcf91Updates.description: Virtual Volumes are deprecated in VCF 9.1 and will be removed in a future release, with migration to vSAN, NFS or Fibre Channel advised on the same timeline as the upgrade.
vcf91Updates.impact: Any design that would have used vVols as a transitional storage model must instead plan a migration path, which reinforces vSAN ESA as the target storage model for both the management and workload domains.

title: The Management Domain
summary: The management domain is the first thing VCF builds and the thing everything else depends on. It hosts the instance's control plane (SDDC Manager, management vCenter, management NSX) and, in the first instance of a fleet, the fleet-level services (VCF Operations, VCF Automation, VCF management services, identity broker, licence server). Design work here is choosing where the domain lives, how large the fleet is, whether the management components run in high availability mode, what storage and cluster model to use, and how identity and PKI are anchored externally.

components.name: VCF Private Cloud Hierarchy
components.what: VCF 9 defines a five-level taxonomy. A VCF private cloud is the highest management and consumption boundary and can contain one or more fleets. A VCF fleet is the environment managed by one set of fleet-level components, namely a single VCF Operations instance and a single VCF Automation instance, and contains one or more instances plus optionally standalone vCenter instances. A VCF instance is a discrete deployment with its own SDDC Manager, management vCenter and management NSX. A VCF domain is a lifecycle and isolation boundary inside an instance, either the mandatory management domain or a VI workload domain. A vSphere cluster is where ESX capacity lives, inside a domain.
components.how: The fleet-level components physically run in the management domain of the first instance in the fleet, which is why the first instance is architecturally special and why its availability and sizing decisions have fleet-wide consequences. Each additional instance still gets its own SDDC Manager, management vCenter and management NSX, and may deploy collectors for observability. Because a fleet is defined by one VCF Operations and one VCF Automation instance, fleet scope is a real design decision: it sets the blast radius of the shared services and the latency budget between those services and everything they manage.
components.why: Broadcom formalised this hierarchy in VCF 9 to separate what is shared from what is local. Centralising operations, automation, identity, licensing and lifecycle orchestration at the fleet level removes per-instance duplication and gives one console across the estate; keeping vCenter, NSX and SDDC Manager instance-local preserves lifecycle independence and failure isolation. Use the fleet boundary to reflect an operational and latency boundary, not an organisational chart.
components.examTip: Memorise the order: private cloud, fleet, instance, domain, vSphere cluster. Know that fleet-level components (VCF Operations and VCF Automation) live in the management domain of the first instance, and that a fleet has exactly one of each.

components.name: Fleet Blueprint and Deployment Models
components.what: Broadcom publishes fleet deployment models, sometimes called fleet design blueprints, describing supported topologies: single-site (single availability zone) centralised management, multi-availability-zone, and multi-region or multi-site models. Each model specifies the placement of fleet components, the supported cluster models, and the availability characteristics that follow.
components.how: You select a blueprint by matching it to the availability and latency facts of the estate. A single-site model uses one VCF Operations and one VCF Automation instance to manage everything, giving the lowest operational complexity and the strongest consistency, and accepting that an availability zone or region failure affects the whole fleet. Multi-zone and multi-region models distribute components to survive a zone loss, at the cost of manual post-installation work, additional latency constraints between components, and generally a second instance to act as a starting point for a new primary management domain. Fleet placement must respect the latency budget between the fleet components and everything they manage, so the fleet should sit in a low-latency, high-bandwidth segment. In 9.1 Broadcom refreshed the blueprints and publishes fleet latency diagrams.
components.why: The blueprints exist so architects do not have to invent management-plane topology from first principles, and so support boundaries are clear. Choosing a blueprint that overshoots the customer's actual availability requirement is a common and expensive error, because multi-region management planes carry real ongoing operational cost.
components.examTip: For a single-site customer with no validated second site, the correct answer is a single-site fleet blueprint. Do not select a multi-region model unless the requirements and the facts (two independent sites, latency, quorum) support it.

components.name: High Availability Appliance Mode
components.what: High availability mode for the VCF management components means deploying them as multi-node clusters rather than single appliances. VCF Operations in its high availability model is a three-node cluster comprising a primary node, a replica node and a data node. The identity broker in appliance mode is likewise a three-node cluster. Both support scale-up of node size and scale-out of additional nodes.
components.how: In the default non-highly-available model, VCF Operations runs as a single appliance and depends on vSphere HA to restart it after a host failure, which means a service interruption. In the high availability model the three-node cluster provides data redundancy and rapid recovery from a single node failure, optionally fronted by an external load balancer for distributed user interface access. Node size is selected from XS through XL based on the forecast virtual machine and object count across every connected instance, and an anti-affinity rule separating the cluster's virtual machines must be created after deployment so the nodes do not share a host. If an external load balancer is used, it needs its own IP address and FQDN, and every node FQDN plus the load balancer FQDN must appear in the certificate's subject alternative names.
components.why: Broadcom offers the mode as a deliberate trade-off. The management plane is not in the workload data path, so its loss does not stop running virtual machines, but it does stop operations, automation, monitoring and lifecycle work. Where the customer's operating model depends on those functions being continuously available, the extra appliances and complexity are justified; where a short vSphere HA restart is acceptable, they are not.
components.examTip: High availability mode equals three-node appliance clusters. Remember the node roles for VCF Operations (primary, replica, data), that sizing is driven by forecast VM and object count, and that you must add a separate-virtual-machines anti-affinity rule after deployment.

components.name: VCF Identity Broker
components.what: The identity broker is the fleet's federated authentication component, the successor to Workspace ONE Access in the VCF lineage. It brokers authentication between VCF components and enterprise identity providers, giving one single sign-on experience across VCF Operations, VCF Automation, vCenter and the rest of the platform.
components.how: It has two deployment modes. Embedded mode uses the identity broker embedded in the management domain vCenter, which is simple but makes that vCenter a single point of failure for authentication and Broadcom's guidance is to connect one embedded broker per instance. Appliance mode deploys a standalone three-node cluster with a built-in internal load balancer, tolerates a single node failure, and can serve up to five VCF instances from one broker. Appliance mode is the recommendation for production and is required if more than one instance must share a broker or if some components cannot reach the management domain vCenter. In 9.1 an identity broker is deployed automatically during installation or upgrade in the first management domain, additional brokers can be added per instance as a day-two action, and small-size deployments are explicitly not for production because they lack service redundancy.
components.why: Broadcom externalises identity so that authentication is a fleet service rather than a per-component configuration, which is what makes consistent role-based access control, auditability and enterprise directory integration achievable. Anchoring on the enterprise identity provider also means account lifecycle, multi-factor authentication and password policy stay where the security team already manages them.
components.examTip: For fleet-wide single sign-on the answer is the external or appliance-mode identity broker, not per-component local accounts and not the embedded broker. Know the appliance cluster is three nodes and that one broker can serve up to five instances.

components.name: VMCA and External Certificate Authority
components.what: The VMware Certificate Authority (VMCA) is the certificate authority embedded in vCenter that can issue and manage certificates for platform components out of the box. The alternative is to anchor the platform's public key infrastructure on an external enterprise certificate authority, either by having the external authority issue component certificates directly or by making VMCA a subordinate of it.
components.how: With VMCA acting as the root, components trust a certificate authority that exists only inside the platform, so every client, browser and integration must be taught to trust it. With an external enterprise authority, certificates chain to a root the organisation already trusts and already governs, and issuance follows the enterprise process for key length, algorithm, validity period, revocation and audit. In practice this means generating certificate signing requests for each component FQDN, including all subject alternative names, and importing signed certificates. Where a load balancer fronts a cluster, its FQDN must also appear in the subject alternative names.
components.why: Broadcom supports both because the choice is a compliance question rather than a technical one. Regulated environments, including anything under PCI DSS, generally require certificates issued and governed by the enterprise public key infrastructure with defined revocation and audit paths, which VMCA as a self-contained root cannot provide. VMCA remains a reasonable choice for lab, proof-of-concept or environments with no external public key infrastructure requirement.
components.examTip: If the scenario mentions public key infrastructure governance, PCI or any compliance regime, the answer is the external certificate authority. Remember that subject alternative names must cover every node FQDN plus any load balancer FQDN.

components.name: SDDC Manager
components.what: SDDC Manager is the instance-level appliance that adds infrastructure automation workflows to the platform: commissioning hosts, creating and expanding domains and clusters, and orchestrating instance lifecycle. It lives in the management domain of every instance and exposes an API that remains the route to operations the user interface does not cover, such as stretching a cluster.
components.how: SDDC Manager holds the inventory of hosts, clusters and domains for its instance and drives the workflows that change them. In VCF 9 those workflows surface through VCF Operations rather than through a separate SDDC Manager console, and lifecycle orchestration is co-ordinated at the fleet level. The API remains essential for advanced operations: stretching a vSAN cluster, for instance, is performed by validating and then submitting a cluster stretch specification to the clusters API rather than through a wizard.
components.why: Broadcom keeps SDDC Manager instance-scoped because infrastructure change is an instance concern with an instance blast radius, while observability and consumption are fleet concerns. Separating them lets one console present the whole estate while change control stays bounded to a single deployment.
components.examTip: SDDC Manager is per instance, not per fleet, and it lives in the management domain. In 9.1 its user interface is deprecated and lifecycle work moves into VCF Operations, but the SDDC Manager API remains the mechanism for advanced operations.

keyFacts: Hierarchy order: VCF private cloud, VCF fleet, VCF instance, VCF domain, vSphere cluster.
A fleet is defined by exactly one VCF Operations instance and one VCF Automation instance, and those fleet components run in the management domain of the first instance.
Every instance has its own SDDC Manager, management vCenter and management NSX; the management domain is mandatory in every instance.
The management domain is created by the VCF Installer and does not host user workloads.
High availability mode for VCF Operations is a three-node cluster: primary, replica and data node.

VCF Operations node size (XS to XL) is chosen from the forecast virtual machine and object count across all connected instances, and a separate-virtual-machines anti-affinity rule must be added after deployment.
The identity broker has two modes: embedded in management domain vCenter, or appliance mode as a three-node cluster with an internal load balancer.
One appliance-mode identity broker can serve up to five VCF instances; embedded mode is recommended as one per instance.

External certificate authority is the correct choice where public key infrastructure governance or compliance such as PCI applies; VMCA is a self-contained root that every client must be taught to trust.
A hardware compatibility listing proves supportability, not fitness for the workload.
attentionItems: Assuming the fleet-level components are distributed. They run in the management domain of the first instance, which makes that instance's availability a fleet-wide concern.
Selecting a multi-region or multi-availability-zone fleet blueprint without two validated independent sites, a measured latency budget and a witness location.

Believing high availability mode protects workloads. It protects the management plane; running virtual machines are unaffected by its loss, but operations, automation, monitoring and lifecycle work stop.
Deploying the three-node VCF Operations cluster and forgetting the anti-affinity rule, leaving all three nodes able to land on one host.
Using the embedded identity broker in production where authentication must survive a management vCenter outage or serve multiple instances.
Omitting load balancer and node FQDNs from certificate subject alternative names, which breaks trust for cluster access.
Confusing instance scope with fleet scope: SDDC Manager, vCenter and NSX are instance-level; VCF Operations, VCF Automation and identity are fleet-level.
Assuming the SDDC Manager user interface is the path for lifecycle work in 9.1. It is deprecated; lifecycle moves to VCF Operations while the API remains for advanced operations.

designDecisions.question: Should the management domain be built on the newly acquired hardware?
designDecisions.recommendation: Build the management domain on the new hardware.
designDecisions.rationale: The management domain is the foundation for the entire instance and, as the first instance, for the fleet's shared services. Building it on new, fully compatible all-NVMe hardware gives a supported baseline that meets VCF 9 requirements, isolates the build from the running production estate, and avoids inheriting the firmware and lifecycle state of hardware due for retirement.
designDecisions.alternative: Reusing or converging existing hardware for the management domain was rejected because it would couple the platform's foundation to end-of-life equipment and to the existing environment's maintenance windows, and would remove the ability to fall back during migration.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Availability improves because the foundation is new and validated and the build does not disturb production. Manageability improves via a single consistent baseline. Recoverability improves because the legacy environment remains available as a fallback. Cost increases and there is a temporary dual-running period.
relatedComponents: vSAN ReadyNode and the Compatibility Guide

designDecisions.question: What fleet deployment model should be used?
designDecisions.recommendation: Use a single-site (single availability zone) fleet blueprint with one VCF Operations instance and one VCF Automation instance.
designDecisions.rationale: The estate is a single site and no second independent availability zone has been validated for latency, power and network independence or witness placement. A single-site centralised management model gives the lowest operational complexity, consistent management across all domains and instances, and satisfies the stated requirements. It also keeps the fleet components in a low-latency, high-bandwidth segment close to everything they manage.
designDecisions.alternative: Multi-availability-zone and multi-region blueprints were rejected because no requirement calls for surviving a site loss at the management plane, the second-site facts required to support them are unvalidated, and they impose additional manual configuration, latency constraints and ongoing operational cost.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Manageability and cost benefit strongly from a single centralised management plane. Availability and recoverability are bounded: a site-level event affects the whole fleet, which must be recorded as an accepted risk with backup and restore as the mitigation. Performance benefits from low latency between fleet components and managed objects.

designDecisions.question: Should the VCF management components be deployed in high availability mode?
designDecisions.recommendation: Deploy the management components in high availability mode, as three-node appliance clusters, with anti-affinity separating the nodes.
designDecisions.rationale: High availability mode gives data redundancy and rapid recovery from a single node failure for the fleet's shared services, rather than relying on a vSphere HA restart with an associated service interruption. Because the fleet components in the first instance serve the whole estate, an outage of VCF Operations or the identity broker stops monitoring, automation, lifecycle and authentication work across every domain, which is a disproportionate operational impact for a single appliance failure.
designDecisions.alternative: The default single-appliance model relying on vSphere HA was rejected for the fleet components because it accepts a service interruption on every host or appliance failure. It remains defensible where the customer explicitly accepts management-plane downtime and wants the smaller footprint, which is why confidence is medium-high rather than high.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Availability of the management plane improves substantially. Recoverability improves through node-level redundancy. Manageability is mixed: fewer outages to handle, but more appliances, more certificate subject alternative names, an optional external load balancer and post-deployment anti-affinity configuration. Performance is neutral. Cost and resource consumption in the management domain increase.

designDecisions.question: Which storage model should the management domain cluster use?
designDecisions.recommendation: Use vSAN ESA for the management domain cluster.
designDecisions.rationale: vSAN ESA on the new all-NVMe ReadyNodes keeps the management plane's storage self-contained, policy-driven and lifecycle-managed with the platform, and removes any dependency on the end-of-life Fibre Channel SAN. Space-efficient erasure coding delivers the required resilience without mirroring's capacity overhead.
designDecisions.alternative: External Fibre Channel storage was rejected because it is end of life and would make the platform's own control plane dependent on retiring hardware. vSAN OSA was rejected because the hardware is all-NVMe and OSA would forgo ESA's performance and efficiency.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Availability and recoverability improve by eliminating an external storage dependency for the management plane. Performance improves on single-tier NVMe. Manageability improves through one storage architecture and policy model. Security is unchanged, with encryption available via policy.

designDecisions.question: Should the management domain cluster use a Layer 3 multi-rack model or a single-rack model?
designDecisions.recommendation: Use the Layer 3 multi-rack model if the racks are validated as independent power, cooling and network failure domains; otherwise use the single-rack model.
designDecisions.rationale: Distributing the management cluster's hosts across independent racks means a rack-level failure does not take the management plane down, which complements the high availability appliance decision. The benefit is entirely contingent on rack independence, and Broadcom's guidance notes the single-rack model is supported for management domains, so the multi-rack complexity must be earned by a real facilities fact.
designDecisions.alternative: A single-rack management cluster was not rejected outright; it is the correct answer where the cluster fits in one rack and rack independence cannot be demonstrated, and it avoids per-rack subnets, TEP VLANs and gateway redundancy.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Availability improves only if rack independence is genuine. Manageability degrades through additional per-rack network configuration and IP management. Performance is broadly neutral, with inter-rack traffic traversing the spine. Cost rises modestly.

designDecisions.question: Should storage traffic be separated onto its own vSphere Distributed Switch, or should a single VDS carry all traffic types?
designDecisions.recommendation: Use a single VDS carrying all traffic types with per-traffic-type VLANs and port groups, unless measured bandwidth or an isolation requirement justifies a separate storage VDS.
designDecisions.rationale: A single VDS with distinct VLANs and port groups per traffic type already provides logical separation, independent MTU and teaming policy, and is significantly simpler to operate and lifecycle. Physical separation onto a second VDS only pays for itself when uplink bandwidth is genuinely contended or when a security or compliance requirement demands separate physical paths for storage.
designDecisions.alternative: A dedicated storage VDS was rejected as the default because it consumes additional uplinks and host NIC ports, doubles switch configuration surface, and delivers isolation the customer has not required. It should be revisited if bandwidth measurement shows contention, which is a live concern given the observed 9 Gbps peak on 10 Gb links.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Manageability improves with one switch object and one configuration surface. Performance is adequate provided uplink bandwidth is sized with headroom, and is the risk that would reverse this decision. Availability is unchanged given redundant uplinks. Security relies on VLAN separation rather than physical separation. Cost is lower.

designDecisions.question: How should authentication and single sign-on be provided across the fleet?
designDecisions.recommendation: Use an external, appliance-mode VCF Identity Broker federated to the enterprise identity provider for fleet-wide single sign-on.
designDecisions.rationale: Appliance mode deploys a three-node cluster with an internal load balancer that tolerates a single node failure, can serve up to five VCF instances, and does not depend on the management domain vCenter being available for authentication. Federating to the enterprise identity provider keeps account lifecycle, multi-factor authentication and password policy under existing security governance, and gives one consistent single sign-on and role-based access control experience across VCF Operations, VCF Automation and vCenter.
designDecisions.alternative: The embedded identity broker in management domain vCenter was rejected because it creates a single point of failure for authentication and is guided as one per instance. Per-component local accounts were rejected outright because they defeat centralised access control, auditability and enterprise password policy.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Security improves substantially through central identity, enterprise policy enforcement and auditability. Availability of authentication improves via the three-node cluster. Manageability improves through one access-control model, at the cost of additional appliances to lifecycle. Performance is neutral.

designDecisions.question: Should platform certificates be issued by VMCA or by an external enterprise certificate authority?
designDecisions.recommendation: Issue platform certificates from the external enterprise certificate authority.
designDecisions.rationale: The environment is subject to public key infrastructure governance and compliance obligations, which require certificates that chain to a trusted enterprise root with defined issuance, key strength, validity, revocation and audit processes. Using the enterprise authority means clients, browsers and integrations already trust the chain, and certificate lifecycle stays inside the existing security process.
designDecisions.alternative: VMCA as the root was rejected because it is a self-contained authority every client must be explicitly taught to trust and it sits outside enterprise certificate governance and revocation, which does not satisfy the compliance requirement. VMCA as a subordinate of the enterprise authority is an acceptable variant where the enterprise process permits it.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Security and compliance improve materially. Manageability is mixed: trust is inherited automatically, but certificate signing requests, subject alternative name management and renewal become an ongoing operational task tied to the enterprise process. Availability carries a new risk if certificates expire unnoticed, so renewal monitoring becomes a day-two requirement.

vcf91Updates.title: VCF Management Services replaces Aria Suite Lifecycle and the fleet management appliance
vcf91Updates.description: VCF 9.1 introduces VCF management services, a common containerised runtime hosting fleet-level and instance-level components: fleet lifecycle, SDDC lifecycle, software depot, identity broker, log management, Salt master and Salt RaaS, and real-time metrics. These replace the VCF Operations fleet management appliance and the former Aria Suite Lifecycle. Aria Suite Lifecycle, VMware Identity Manager and Aria Operations for Logs have no 9.1 upgrade path; their roles move into VCF management services. Deployment requires a dedicated /27 CIDR for the services runtime plus unique FQDNs for the runtime, fleet components, instance components, identity broker and licence server, and a licence server appliance is mandatory.
vcf91Updates.impact: The management domain's component inventory and sizing change: fewer standalone appliances, one shared runtime, and new network and DNS prerequisites that must be captured in the planning workbook. DD-603 on high availability now applies to the services runtime and its hosted components rather than to a set of independent appliances, and backup and recovery become unified across the hosted components.

vcf91Updates.title: SDDC Manager user interface deprecated
vcf91Updates.description: The SDDC Manager user interface is deprecated in VCF 9.1 and lifecycle work moves into VCF Operations. The SDDC Manager appliance and its API remain, and the API is still the route for advanced operations such as stretching a cluster.
vcf91Updates.impact: Operational runbooks and role-based access design must target VCF Operations as the lifecycle console rather than SDDC Manager, which reinforces the identity and access decisions in DD-607 and raises the operational importance of VCF Operations availability in DD-603.

vcf91Updates.title: VCF Installer fully replaces Cloud Builder
vcf91Updates.description: VCF Installer completely replaces Cloud Builder. Deployment moves from the Cloud Builder spreadsheet to a curated, guided set of steps in the VCF Operations user interface, with support for importing JSON configuration templates. Converging an existing vCenter and ESX 8.0 Update 3 or later environment into a management domain is integrated into VCF Installer, and importing existing vSphere into a VI workload domain is done from VCF Operations.
vcf91Updates.impact: The build method for DD-601 changes: converge and import are first-class, integrated pathways rather than separate tools, which makes reuse of existing infrastructure a more credible alternative to evaluate even where new hardware remains the recommendation.

vcf91Updates.title: Fleet scale to 5000 hosts and four times faster parallel upgrades
vcf91Updates.description: A single instance can now manage up to 5000 ESX hosts, doubled from 2500 in VCF 9.0, and parallel patching capacity rises from 64 to 256 clusters upgraded concurrently. VCF 9.1 also adds fleet-wide policy enforcement with configuration drift visibility, and upgrade pre-checks that evaluate system health and resource capacity before an upgrade runs.
vcf91Updates.impact: Fleet and instance boundary decisions such as DD-602 can be driven by operational and latency considerations rather than by scale ceilings, and maintenance window sizing improves substantially, which weakens one of the historical arguments for splitting an estate across multiple fleets.

title: The Workload Domain
summary: A VI workload domain is the lifecycle and isolation boundary where consumer workloads actually run, with its own vCenter and optionally its own NSX Manager cluster. For the development platform the design creates a new workload domain and migrates into it, then works through cluster and rack model, storage architecture and FTT policy, network model (VPC), Edge cluster placement, and placement control through DRS groups and anti-affinity rules. Sizing must come from measured evidence, not from allocated values.

components.name: VI Workload Domain
components.what: A workload domain is a domain inside a VCF instance dedicated to running consumer workloads, as distinct from the management domain which hosts the platform's own components. Each workload domain has its own vCenter instance, one or more vSphere clusters, and an NSX Manager cluster that it either owns or shares.
components.how: Workload domains are created from VCF Operations. For the first workload domain, VCF Operations deploys a vCenter instance and an NSX Manager instance into the management domain; for each additional workload domain it deploys another vCenter, and you choose whether to share an existing NSX Manager cluster (with another workload domain or with the management domain) or to deploy a new one. All clusters in all domains sharing an NSX Manager also share the overlay transport zone, which is why NSX sharing is an isolation decision and not just a footprint decision.
