Capacity is added by commissioning hosts and expanding clusters, and vSphere Supervisor can be enabled during workload domain creation to turn the domain into a consumption platform.
components.why: Broadcom separates workload domains from the management domain so that workload lifecycle, upgrade cadence, resource contention and failure domains are decoupled from the platform's control plane. Creating a separate domain per distinct workload class, such as development versus production, gives independent upgrade windows and a smaller blast radius, at the cost of an additional vCenter to operate.
components.examTip: Remember that the management domain never hosts user workloads, that each workload domain gets its own vCenter, and that NSX Manager can be shared or dedicated. The first workload domain's vCenter and NSX Manager appliances are deployed into the management domain.

components.name: VPC Networking
components.what: A Virtual Private Cloud in NSX is an isolated, self-contained domain of networking resources, with its own address space, subnets, routing, outbound network address translation and services, that can be associated with one or more isolated compute domains (vSphere namespaces). It is the default and recommended workload network model for Supervisor in VCF 9.
components.how: The VPC framework is natively multi-tenant. A provider or VI administrator creates VPCs in a default space, or tenant organisations create their own VPCs and map vSphere namespaces to them. The NSX Container Plugin automatically creates the VPC, load balancer, SNAT address and default subnet sets for a namespace, and VPC constructs are exposed as Kubernetes custom resources through the Supervisor API, so consumers create subnets declaratively. VPCs are configured with default outbound network address translation so private workloads can reach external resources. A VPC spans a single region, so namespaces in different regions always map to different VPCs. Different VPCs are used where workloads need network segregation, while private transit gateway subnets allow controlled communication between them; where no separation is needed, one VPC can serve many namespaces.
components.why: Broadcom made VPC the recommended model because tenant self-service networking cannot depend on a network team provisioning VLANs and segments. VPC gives each tenant a cloud-like network they can shape themselves, inside guardrails the provider sets, and it is a prerequisite for the full VCF Automation All Apps capability set. Other stacks (VDS-backed, NSX classic Tier-0/Tier-1 segments) are supported but do not unlock the complete capability set.
components.examTip: VPC equals tenant self-service, isolated networking, and it is the prerequisite for All Apps organizations. Know that VPCs are region-scoped and that the NSX Container Plugin automatically provisions VPC, load balancer, SNAT and subnet sets for a namespace.

components.name: NSX Edge Cluster
components.what: NSX Edge nodes are the transport nodes that host centralised networking services: north-south routing via Tier-0 gateways, BGP peering with the physical fabric, network address translation, load balancing, VPN and gateway firewalling. They are grouped into an Edge cluster, which can be deployed into the management domain, into a workload domain's cluster, or onto hosts dedicated to Edge duty.
components.how: Edge nodes have their own overlay TEP network (edge TEP) and their own uplink VLANs to the fabric, and they peer with the leaf switches using BGP to advertise overlay networks northbound. Because all north-south traffic for the domain traverses the Edge cluster, its bandwidth, node size and node count are sized from measured north-south throughput, not from workload count. Placement is the design decision: a dedicated Edge cluster on its own hosts isolates Edge lifecycle and failure from the workloads, whereas a collapsed Edge sharing workload hosts saves hardware but couples the two. For rack-level resilience, Broadcom defines a rack-fault-tolerant Edge cluster model paired with the Layer 3 multi-rack cluster model.
components.why: Broadcom separates the Edge from the distributed data plane because some functions genuinely cannot be distributed: they need a deterministic point of policy enforcement and a peering relationship with the physical network. Dedicating hosts to the Edge cluster is the standard recommendation for production because Edge upgrades, failures and bandwidth demands then do not disturb tenant workloads.
components.examTip: The reason to dedicate an Edge cluster is isolation of lifecycle and failure domain, plus predictable north-south bandwidth. Note that in 9.1 the distributed EVPN-VXLAN option can remove centralised gateway appliances from the data path, which changes this sizing conversation.

components.name: DRS VM and Host Groups
components.what: DRS groups are named collections of virtual machines or of hosts within a single cluster, used as the operands of VM-Host affinity rules. A VM-Host rule states whether the members of a VM group can or must run on the members of a host group.
components.how: You create a VM DRS group and a host DRS group, then define a rule combining them with two choices: requirement strength and polarity. Strength is either 'must' (a hard requirement DRS and HA will not violate) or 'should' (a preference DRS will try to honour and will break to keep workloads running). Polarity is either 'run on' (affinity) or 'not run on' (anti-affinity). Because these rules are cluster-scoped, every virtual machine and host named must reside in the same cluster, and a virtual machine removed from the cluster loses its group membership even if it is later returned. Typical uses are pinning licence-restricted workloads to specific hosts, keeping a workload class within a rack or availability zone, and steering workloads away from hosts reserved for other purposes.
components.why: Broadcom provides host groups so that placement policy can express facts DRS cannot infer: licensing boundaries, hardware capability such as GPU or specific CPU features, rack or zone locality, and regulatory separation. The must-versus-should distinction exists because a hard rule that HA cannot satisfy will leave virtual machines powered off, which is why 'should' is the safer default unless the constraint is genuinely absolute.
components.examTip: VM-Host rules operate on groups; VM-VM rules operate on individual virtual machines. Know that 'must' rules are enforced even by HA (and can therefore block a restart) while 'should' rules are preferences, and that all objects must be in the same cluster.

components.name: Anti-Affinity Rules
components.what: A VM-VM anti-affinity rule tells DRS to keep the named virtual machines on separate hosts. Its opposite, a VM-VM affinity rule, tries to keep them together. Anti-affinity is the mechanism that stops a clustered application's redundant members from sharing a single host and therefore a single failure.
components.how: You select the individual virtual machines and create a separate-virtual-machines rule; DRS then places and migrates them onto different hosts and avoids consolidating them. This is why Broadcom's high availability guidance for the three-node VCF Operations cluster explicitly requires creating a separate-virtual-machines rule after deployment. Combining rule types is the normal production pattern: host groups keep a workload class inside the right rack or hardware boundary, while anti-affinity spreads the redundant members of each application across hosts inside that boundary. Cluster host count must be large enough to satisfy the rules, since an anti-affinity rule across n virtual machines needs at least n usable hosts.
components.why: Broadcom separates these rules because application-level redundancy is invisible to the platform: vSphere cannot know that two virtual machines are database replicas. Anti-affinity is how the architect tells it. Without the rule, DRS may consolidate both replicas onto one host for efficiency and silently convert application redundancy into a single point of failure.
components.examTip: The examinable pattern is VM/Host groups plus anti-affinity rules used together: groups for boundary and capability placement, anti-affinity for spreading redundant application members. Also remember anti-affinity needs enough hosts to satisfy it.

keyFacts: Each workload domain has its own vCenter; NSX Manager can be dedicated to the domain or shared with another domain or the management domain.
The management domain never hosts user workloads.
The first workload domain's vCenter and NSX Manager appliances are deployed into the management domain.
600 virtual machines is the post-growth figure when the current 200 development virtual machines triple.
Allocated memory is what someone requested; it is dangerous to extrapolate from and must be replaced with measured consumption plus growth.
VPC is the default and recommended Supervisor workload network in VCF 9 and a prerequisite for the full All Apps capability set.
VPCs are region-scoped, so namespaces in different regions always map to different VPCs.
The NSX Container Plugin automatically creates the VPC, load balancer, SNAT address and default subnet sets for a namespace.
A dedicated NSX Edge cluster isolates Edge lifecycle and failure domain and gives predictable north-south bandwidth.
VM-Host affinity rules act on groups and support must/should and run-on/not-run-on; VM-VM anti-affinity rules act on individual virtual machines.
All objects named in a DRS rule must be in the same cluster, and an anti-affinity rule across n virtual machines needs at least n usable hosts.
attentionItems: Sizing from allocated CPU and memory. Allocation reflects requests, not consumption; extrapolating it multiplies the original over-provisioning.
Confusing VM-VM rules with VM-Host rules. Only VM-Host rules use DRS groups.
Using 'must' rules casually. A hard rule HA cannot satisfy leaves virtual machines powered off after a failure.
Creating anti-affinity rules the cluster cannot satisfy because there are not enough hosts.
Sharing an NSX Manager cluster without acknowledging that the domains then share an overlay transport zone and a lifecycle.
Collapsing the Edge into the workload cluster and then discovering that Edge upgrades and north-south bursts affect tenant workloads.
Choosing a VDS-backed or NSX classic workload network and then expecting the full VCF Automation All Apps capability set, which requires VPC.
Assuming a workload domain gets rack resilience automatically. That comes from the multi-rack cluster model plus a rack-fault-tolerant Edge model, and only if racks are independent.

designDecisions.question: Should the development workload be hosted in a new workload domain, or placed into the management domain or an existing environment?
designDecisions.recommendation: Create a new VI workload domain for the development platform and migrate the existing development workloads into it.
designDecisions.rationale: A dedicated workload domain gives the development platform its own vCenter, its own lifecycle and upgrade cadence, and a failure and resource-contention boundary separate from the management plane and from any other workload class. Building it new and migrating into it also means the existing environment keeps running during the transition and remains available as a fallback, which is what makes a staged, wave-based migration possible.
designDecisions.alternative: Placing development workloads in the management domain was rejected outright because the management domain does not host user workloads. Upgrading or converging the existing environment in place was rejected because it couples the new platform to the old estate's maintenance windows and hardware lifecycle and removes the fallback position during migration.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Availability improves through isolation from the management plane and from other workload classes, and because migration does not disturb the running environment. Manageability is mixed: independent lifecycle and upgrade windows are gained, but an additional vCenter must be operated. Recoverability improves because the source environment remains as a fallback. Cost increases during the dual-running period.

designDecisions.question: Should the workload domain clusters use the Layer 3 multi-rack model?
designDecisions.recommendation: Use the Layer 3 multi-rack cluster model where racks are validated as independent failure domains; otherwise use the single-rack model.
designDecisions.rationale: Multi-rack lets a workload cluster survive the loss of a rack and grow horizontally beyond one rack's capacity, which matters given the projected growth to around 600 virtual machines. The Layer 3 model is Broadcom's supported multi-rack approach for workload domains, using per-rack VLANs and subnets with highly available first-hop gateways. The benefit depends entirely on the racks being independent for power, cooling and network.
designDecisions.alternative: A single-rack cluster model was not rejected outright and remains correct where capacity fits in one rack or rack independence is unproven. A Layer 2 stretched multi-rack approach was rejected because it reintroduces large stretched broadcast domains that the overlay exists to avoid.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Availability improves materially if rack independence is genuine and not at all if it is not. Performance is broadly neutral, with inter-rack traffic traversing the spine. Manageability degrades through per-rack subnet, TEP VLAN and gateway management, and the Edge cluster must adopt the matching rack-fault-tolerant model. Cost rises modestly.

designDecisions.question: Which storage architecture should the workload domain clusters use?
designDecisions.recommendation: Use vSAN ESA for the workload domain clusters.
designDecisions.rationale: ESA on all-NVMe ReadyNodes gives the workload domain a scale-out datastore whose service levels are set per workload through SPBM, so a single cluster can serve differentiated resilience and space-efficiency requirements. It retires the dependency on the end-of-life 8 Gbps Fibre Channel SAN and matches the management domain's storage architecture, keeping one operational model across the instance.
designDecisions.alternative: Continuing on the existing Fibre Channel SAN was rejected on end-of-life and bandwidth grounds. vSAN OSA was rejected because the hardware is all-NVMe and OSA forgoes ESA's erasure-coding performance, adaptive RAID-5 and 9.1 efficiency features. A new external array was rejected as an unnecessary second storage lifecycle and failure domain.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Performance improves on single-tier NVMe with erasure coding at mirroring-like performance. Manageability improves via one storage architecture and per-workload policy rather than datastore tiers. Availability depends on the FTT policy set in DD-705. Cost is driven by the capacity overhead of that policy choice.
relatedComponents: Storage Policy and Failures To Tolerate (FTT)

designDecisions.question: Should storage traffic and workload traffic be separated onto different vSphere Distributed Switches in the workload domain?
designDecisions.recommendation: Use a single VDS with separate VLANs and port groups per traffic type, and revisit only if measured uplink contention or an isolation requirement emerges.
designDecisions.rationale: Distinct VLANs and port groups on one VDS already give logical separation with independent MTU and teaming policy, and one switch object is materially simpler to operate and lifecycle. Physical separation earns its cost only when uplink bandwidth is genuinely contended or a compliance requirement demands separate physical paths, neither of which is currently a stated requirement.
designDecisions.alternative: A dedicated storage VDS was rejected as the default because it consumes additional host NIC ports and uplinks and doubles the switch configuration surface. It stays on the table because the observed 9 Gbps peak on 10 Gb links shows the uplinks already run close to capacity, so bandwidth measurement after migration may reverse this decision.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Manageability improves with one configuration surface. Performance is the risk: vSAN traffic now shares uplinks with workload traffic, so headroom must be verified. Availability is unchanged with redundant uplinks. Security relies on VLAN rather than physical separation. Cost is lower.

designDecisions.question: What failures-to-tolerate policy and data placement scheme should the development workloads use: mirroring or erasure coding?
designDecisions.recommendation: Use FTT=1 with RAID-5 erasure coding as the default policy for development workloads, sizing the cluster at one host above the policy minimum, and reserve mirroring for any workload with a specific requirement.
designDecisions.rationale: In ESA, erasure coding performs at mirroring-like levels, so RAID-5 gives the same effective performance at 1.25x to 1.5x capacity overhead instead of mirroring's 2x. FTT=1 is proportionate for a development platform, and SPBM allows any individual workload that needs more resilience to be given FTT=2 RAID-6 without changing the cluster. Running one host above the policy minimum (four hosts for FTT=1 RAID-5) means resilience can be restored during a failure or maintenance window.
designDecisions.alternative: RAID-1 mirroring was rejected because in ESA it buys no meaningful performance advantage and doubles capacity consumption; Broadcom reserves it for stretched-cluster site resilience and two-node host resilience. FTT=2 as the default was rejected as disproportionate for development workloads, though it remains available per workload through policy. Confidence is medium because the choice depends on the capacity and IOPS evidence still being validated and, in 9.1, on whether Auto-RAID is adopted.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Cost and usable capacity improve substantially versus mirroring. Availability is set deliberately at single-failure tolerance, which is the accepted risk for a development platform. Performance is equivalent to mirroring in ESA. Manageability improves because one default policy plus targeted exceptions is simpler than multiple datastore tiers.
relatedComponents: Storage Policy and Failures To Tolerate (FTT)

designDecisions.question: Which workload network model should the workload domain use?
designDecisions.recommendation: Use the VPC network model (VCF Networking with VPC) for Supervisor and tenant workloads.
designDecisions.rationale: VPC is the default and recommended Supervisor workload network in VCF 9 and the prerequisite for VCF Automation All Apps organizations. It gives each tenant an isolated, self-service network with its own address space, subnets, routing and outbound network address translation, provisioned declaratively through Kubernetes custom resources by the NSX Container Plugin, inside guardrails the provider sets. That is exactly what a self-service development platform requires.
designDecisions.alternative: VDS-backed and NSX classic Tier-0/Tier-1 segment networking are supported but were rejected because they do not unlock the full VCF 9 capability set and they leave network provisioning as a ticket to the network team, defeating the self-service requirement.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Manageability improves markedly through declarative, tenant-driven networking instead of manual VLAN and segment provisioning. Security improves through per-tenant network isolation and distributed policy. Performance is neutral. Availability depends on the underlying NSX and Edge design. Manageability also carries a new burden: address space and IP block planning per organisation and VPC.

designDecisions.question: Where should the NSX Edge cluster be placed for the workload domain?
designDecisions.recommendation: Deploy a dedicated NSX Edge cluster rather than collapsing Edge nodes into the workload compute clusters.
designDecisions.rationale: All north-south traffic and all centralised services for the domain pass through the Edge cluster, so its bandwidth demands, failure behaviour and upgrade cadence are different from those of tenant workloads. Dedicating it isolates Edge lifecycle and failure from the workloads and makes north-south bandwidth predictable and independently sizeable. Where the multi-rack Layer 3 cluster model is used, the matching rack-fault-tolerant Edge cluster model applies.
designDecisions.alternative: A collapsed Edge sharing workload hosts was rejected as the default because it couples Edge upgrades and traffic bursts to tenant workloads and makes resource contention hard to reason about. It remains defensible in small environments where the additional hosts cannot be justified, which is why confidence is medium-high rather than high.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Availability improves through failure-domain separation. Manageability improves through independent Edge lifecycle, at the cost of more hosts and another cluster to operate. Performance improves through predictable, dedicated north-south capacity. Cost increases. In 9.1 the distributed EVPN-VXLAN option can reduce the centralised Edge's role in the data path, which should be evaluated before finalising node sizing.

designDecisions.question: How should workload placement be controlled within the workload domain clusters?
designDecisions.recommendation: Use DRS VM and host groups together with VM-VM anti-affinity rules: groups to bind workload classes to the correct hosts, racks or hardware capability, and anti-affinity to spread redundant application members across hosts.
designDecisions.rationale: The platform cannot infer application-level redundancy or licensing and hardware boundaries, so placement policy has to be stated explicitly. Host groups express the boundary (rack, availability zone, licence-restricted or GPU-equipped hosts) while anti-affinity ensures the redundant members of an application do not share a host and therefore a single failure. Preferential 'should' rules are the default so that HA can still restart workloads during a failure, with 'must' reserved for genuinely absolute constraints such as licensing.
designDecisions.alternative: Relying on DRS defaults alone was rejected because DRS optimises for balance and will happily consolidate redundant application members onto one host, silently converting application redundancy into a single point of failure. Using only 'must' rules was rejected because a hard rule that HA cannot satisfy leaves virtual machines powered off.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Availability improves because application redundancy survives a host failure. Manageability requires ongoing rule hygiene, since rules are cluster-scoped and group membership is lost if a virtual machine leaves the cluster. Performance is broadly neutral, though rules constrain DRS's balancing freedom. Cluster host count must be sufficient to satisfy the rules.

vcf91Updates.title: VKS and VM Fast-Deploy
vcf91Updates.description: VCF 9.1 uses linked clone technology to speed up deployment and upgrade of VKS clusters and virtual machines, and adds linked clones of first class disks for fast provisioning of container storage volumes. Broadcom cites provisioning around 70 percent faster with maintenance downtime windows reduced by around 75 percent, and a single Supervisor now supports up to 500 Kubernetes clusters.
vcf91Updates.impact: Provisioning-time service level objectives for the development platform become much easier to meet, which affects the targets instrumented in DD-1003. Higher per-Supervisor cluster scale also means workload domain and Supervisor sizing is less likely to be the limiting factor when the development estate grows.

vcf91Updates.title: Simplified Container-as-a-Service
vcf91Updates.description: Self-service namespace provisioning with registry, ingress, quotas and identity inherited from existing VCF constructs, giving a faster path to running a few containers without standing up and managing a full Kubernetes cluster.
vcf91Updates.impact: The namespace and tenancy decisions carry more weight because namespaces now inherit registry, ingress, quota and identity configuration automatically, so getting the namespace boundary right in DD-903 delivers more value. It also offers a lighter-weight consumption option alongside full VKS clusters.

vcf91Updates.title: VKS multi-interface networking and Istio service mesh
vcf91Updates.description: VKS clusters can be deployed with a secondary network interface, and pods running Antrea CNI can have secondary interfaces, with cluster nodes and pod secondary NICs mapped to VLAN-backed or overlay-backed subnets in an NSX VPC. Istio service mesh is available per VKS cluster in both sidecar and ambient modes, providing mutual TLS between container workloads and the full set of Istio security and traffic management APIs.
vcf91Updates.impact: Use cases previously blocked by single-interface networking, such as traffic isolation, multicast, and direct access to physical systems like NFS storage, are now supported, which adds requirements to VPC address-space and subnet planning under DD-706.

vcf91Updates.title: Mixed organization models on shared infrastructure
vcf91Updates.description: In VCF 9.1 an environment can run the legacy VM Apps organization model alongside the modern All Apps organization model, and both can share the same vCenter and NSX rather than requiring separate infrastructure.
vcf91Updates.impact: A phased adoption path for Supervisor-based consumption becomes viable without duplicating vCenter and NSX, which lowers the cost of the All Apps recommendation in DD-902 and removes an argument for deferring it.

title: AMPRS: Cross-Cutting Quality Evaluation
summary: AMPRS is the lens you apply to every design decision after it is made, to state what the decision bought and what it cost. The five dimensions are Availability, Manageability, Performance, Recoverability and Security. The core discipline is recognising that these trade against each other, that availability and recoverability are different problems needing different mechanisms, and that a topology like a stretched cluster has hard physical prerequisites that must be validated before it can be recommended.

components.name: AMPRS Framework
components.what: AMPRS is the five-dimension evaluation model used throughout the VCF design methodology: Availability (tolerance to component and site failure), Manageability (operational effort, tooling and skills required), Performance (throughput, latency and headroom), Recoverability (ability to restore after data loss or corruption) and Security (identity, encryption, segmentation and compliance).
components.how: Every design decision record carries an AMPRS impact statement naming which dimensions improve, which degrade and by how much. The value comes from the honesty of the degradations. Adding a three-node high availability cluster improves availability and degrades manageability and cost. Choosing erasure coding over mirroring improves cost and capacity efficiency and, in OSA, degrades write performance. Choosing an external certificate authority improves security and degrades manageability by adding a certificate renewal obligation. Because the dimensions conflict, the framework does not produce a single best answer; it produces a documented, defendable trade-off tied back to the non-functional requirements that set the priorities.
components.why: Broadcom uses AMPRS as the connective tissue between requirements and decisions. It stops designs from silently optimising a single dimension, usually availability, at the expense of an operations team's ability to run the result. It also makes design review possible, because a reviewer can check whether the declared trade-offs match the customer's stated priorities.
components.examTip: Know the acronym expansion exactly: Availability, Manageability, Performance, Recoverability, Security. Expect questions asking which dimension a given consequence belongs to, and remember that operational effort and required skills are manageability, not availability.

components.name: High Availability versus Backup and Recovery
components.what: High availability and backup are answers to different questions. High availability limits the duration of an interruption caused by component failure, by having redundancy already in place so a surviving component takes over. Backup and recovery enable restoration of data and configuration after loss, corruption, deletion or compromise, by holding an independent copy that can be brought back.
components.how: vSphere HA restarts virtual machines on surviving hosts after a host failure; vSAN FTT policy keeps object data available through host or device failure; three-node management clusters survive a node loss. None of these protect against a workload being deleted, a database being corrupted, a bad change being applied, or ransomware encrypting data, because every replica faithfully reflects the damage. Backup and recovery address exactly those cases, and they are governed by different targets: recovery point objective (how much data loss is acceptable) and recovery time objective (how long restoration may take). A complete design needs both, and its recoverability statement must cover the platform's own components as well as the workloads, which in 9.1 is simplified because VCF management services share a common runtime with unified backup and recovery.
components.why: Broadcom separates the two because conflating them is one of the most common and most expensive design errors. A customer told they have 'high availability' frequently believes they are protected against data loss, and discovers otherwise during an incident. Stating the distinction explicitly in the recoverability dimension is how the architect prevents that.
components.examTip: The exam phrasing is that high availability limits interruption while backup enables restoration. Redundancy and replication are not backup, because they replicate corruption and deletion faithfully.

components.name: Stretched Cluster
components.what: A vSAN stretched cluster spans two data sites with a third witness site, placing a copy of data at each data site and witness components at the third, so that the loss of a whole site does not lose data or availability. It is the strongest availability topology vSAN offers and also the one with the hardest physical prerequisites.
components.how: The requirements are specific and non-negotiable. Latency between the two data sites must not exceed 5 ms round trip (2.5 ms one way), with at least 10 Gbps and preferably 25 Gbps of bandwidth for vSAN traffic. Latency between the witness site and the data sites must not exceed 200 ms round trip, and the witness needs only around 100 Mbps because it carries metadata, not data. The witness must be a genuinely independent third location, not co-located with either data site, and must never run inside the stretched cluster it arbitrates. Both data sites should hold an equal number of hosts so failover capacity exists, and site-level resilience is the one case where RAID-1 mirroring is still required rather than erasure coding. In VCF the stretch operation is performed through the SDDC Manager API by validating and then submitting a cluster stretch specification, not through a wizard.
components.why: Broadcom sets these bounds because synchronous write acknowledgement across sites is what makes the topology work, and beyond roughly 5 ms round trip the write latency becomes unacceptable to applications. The independent witness exists to break quorum deterministically during a site partition; a witness sharing fate with a data site cannot do that. The design lesson is that a stretched cluster is a facilities and network capability first and a configuration second.
components.examTip: Memorise the three prerequisites: two genuinely independent failure domains, 5 ms round trip or less between data sites, and an independent witness for quorum at up to 200 ms. If a scenario quotes 25 ms between sites, a stretched cluster is not possible and asynchronous replication with backup is the answer.

components.name: RTO and RPO
components.what: Recovery time objective is the maximum acceptable duration between a disruption and service restoration. Recovery point objective is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss, expressed as a time window back from the moment of failure. Together they are the two numbers that define a recoverability requirement.
components.how: The pair drives mechanism selection. A recovery point objective of zero requires synchronous replication, which brings the stretched cluster latency constraint with it. A recovery point objective of minutes suits asynchronous replication or snapshot-based protection. A recovery point objective of hours suits scheduled backup. Recovery time objective drives how the restore is performed and pre-staged: restoring hundreds of terabytes from backup cannot meet a one-hour recovery time objective regardless of the backup product, which is why RTO frequently forces a replication or snapshot approach rather than a restore approach. Both numbers must come from the business per workload class, because a development platform and a payment system rarely share them, and both must be tested rather than assumed.
components.why: Broadcom insists on stating RTO and RPO because they are the only way to make recoverability designable rather than aspirational. They also expose the cost curve honestly: each step towards zero multiplies infrastructure and operational cost, so making the customer choose the number is what keeps the design proportionate.
components.examTip: RPO equals acceptable data loss (how far back), RTO equals acceptable downtime (how long to restore). Do not swap them. Expect a scenario where a stated RPO or RTO rules out a proposed mechanism.

keyFacts: AMPRS equals Availability, Manageability, Performance, Recoverability, Security.
High availability limits the duration of an interruption; backup and recovery enable restoration after loss or corruption.
Replication and redundancy are not backup, because they faithfully replicate deletion, corruption and ransomware encryption.
A vSAN stretched cluster requires two independent failure domains, no more than 5 ms round trip between data sites (2.5 ms one way), and an independent witness site for quorum.
Witness site latency may be up to 200 ms round trip (100 ms one way) and needs only about 100 Mbps because it carries metadata.
vSAN traffic between stretched data sites needs at least 10 Gbps, with 25 Gbps recommended.
The witness must never be co-located with a data site and must never run inside the cluster it arbitrates.
Site-level resilience in a stretched cluster is one of only two cases where RAID-1 mirroring is still required; the other is host resilience in two-node clusters.
Both data sites of a stretched cluster should have an equal host count so failover capacity exists.
In VCF, stretching a cluster is performed through the SDDC Manager API using a cluster stretch specification, not through a user interface wizard.
RPO equals acceptable data loss; RTO equals acceptable time to restore. Both are set per workload class by the business.
Improving one AMPRS dimension almost always costs another; the design decision record must state the degradation, not just the benefit.
attentionItems: Believing high availability protects against data loss. It does not: it protects against component failure.
Recommending a stretched cluster before validating the physical facts. Two independent zones, sub-5 ms round trip and an independent witness are prerequisites, not configuration options.
Placing the witness at one of the data sites, or inside the stretched cluster. Either destroys its ability to break quorum.
Swapping RPO and RTO. RPO looks backwards at data loss; RTO looks forwards at restoration time.
Writing an AMPRS impact statement that lists only benefits. If no dimension degraded, the analysis is incomplete.
Forgetting that manageability includes operational skills and headcount, not just tooling. A design the team cannot run is not a good design.
Overlooking the platform's own recoverability. The management components need a backup and restore plan too.
Assuming an unequal host count across stretched sites is acceptable. Without balanced capacity, a site failure has nowhere to fail over to.

designDecisions.question: Should a stretched cluster be used to provide site-level availability, or should the design rely on high availability within a single site plus backup and recovery?
designDecisions.recommendation: Adopt a stretched cluster only if two independent availability zones are validated for latency, independence and witness placement; otherwise rely on vSphere HA and vSAN FTT policy within the site, plus a tested backup and recovery capability sized to the agreed RTO and RPO.
designDecisions.rationale: A stretched cluster is the only topology that survives a site loss without data loss, but it depends on facts that are currently unvalidated: two genuinely independent failure domains, no more than 5 ms round trip between data sites with at least 10 Gbps of vSAN bandwidth, and an independent third location for the witness at up to 200 ms. Until those are proven, recommending it would be designing on an assumption. Within a single site, vSphere HA plus vSAN FTT policy limits interruption from component and host failure, and backup and recovery covers the loss, corruption and ransomware cases that redundancy cannot.
designDecisions.alternative: Recommending a stretched cluster unconditionally was rejected because the latency, independence and witness prerequisites are unvalidated and the design would fail if any of them proved false. Relying on high availability alone with no backup capability was rejected because redundancy replicates corruption and deletion and therefore provides no recoverability. Confidence is medium because the recommendation is explicitly conditional on validation results that are still outstanding.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Availability is bounded to component and host failure within the single site until a second zone is validated, which must be recorded as an accepted risk. Recoverability is delivered by backup and restore against agreed RTO and RPO targets rather than by site redundancy. Manageability stays substantially lower than a stretched design, which carries witness management, balanced site capacity and API-driven stretch operations. Cost is materially lower. Performance avoids the synchronous cross-site write penalty.
relatedComponents: High Availability versus Backup and Recovery

vcf91Updates.title: On-premises ransomware recovery with CrowdStrike Falcon validation
vcf91Updates.description: VCF 9.1 adds integrated cyber recovery into on-premises VCF isolated clean rooms, with CrowdStrike Falcon endpoint security integration so that recovered workloads are scanned and validated inside the isolated recovery environment before being returned to production. vSAN for Recovery adds efficient replication and native deep snapshot chains for both disaster and ransomware recovery.
vcf91Updates.impact: Recoverability gains a mechanism specifically addressing the case high availability cannot cover, and it does so without moving data off-premises, which matters for data sovereignty and avoids restoration bandwidth costs during an incident. This strengthens the backup-and-recovery half of DD-801 and adds clean-room validation as a step to build into RTO calculations.

vcf91Updates.title: Live patching for TPM-enabled ESX hosts
vcf91Updates.description: Security patches are applied directly to running kernel memory on TPM-enabled hosts, so virtual machines keep running with no maintenance window and no host evacuation. Broadcom states this covers up to 80 percent of patches.
vcf91Updates.impact: The historical tension between security (patch promptly) and availability (avoid maintenance windows) largely disappears for the covered patch classes, which reduces the availability cost of a strong patching posture and shrinks the maintenance window requirement that often drives extra cluster capacity. TPM presence on hosts becomes a hardware design input.

vcf91Updates.title: Partner-validated NVMe stretched cluster solutions
vcf91Updates.description: VCF 9.1 introduces NVMe dispersed namespaces, enabling storage partners to validate and support NVMe-based stretched cluster solutions.
vcf91Updates.impact: Where a second validated availability zone exists, there are now additional supported stretched topologies beyond vSAN stretched clusters, which broadens the option set to re-evaluate under DD-801 without changing the underlying latency and witness prerequisites.

title: Consumption
summary: Consumption is how the platform is handed to its users. VCF Automation sits at the fleet level and presents organizations; All Apps organizations are backed by vSphere Supervisor and use projects and vSphere namespaces as the resource envelopes; VM Service and VKS Service are the mechanisms that let a namespace deliver virtual machines and Kubernetes clusters through one declarative API. The design work is choosing the organization type, drawing namespace boundaries around trust zones, deciding how hard the tenancy boundary needs to be, and laying out Supervisor zones.

components.name: VCF Automation
components.what: VCF Automation is the fleet-level self-service consumption and automation layer of VCF, the successor to Aria Automation and, in the 9.x lineage, also absorbing the Cloud Director tenancy role. A fleet has exactly one VCF Automation instance, running in the management domain of the first instance, and it is built on the vSphere Supervisor platform.
components.how: It exposes a Provider Management Portal for the platform team and Organization Portals for tenants. The provider creates organizations, assigns Supervisor capacity, VM classes, storage classes and network resources to them, and publishes catalogue items. Tenants then consume built-in cloud services on a self-service basis: virtual machines, Kubernetes clusters, networking, volumes, a secret store, databases, Harbor container registries, external DNS, certificates and AI workloads. Because it is a single fleet-level instance, its availability and sizing are fleet-wide concerns and it is one of the components covered by the high availability decision in the management domain.
components.why: Broadcom centralises consumption at the fleet level so that a tenant's experience is uniform across every instance and domain in the estate, and so that governance, quota and chargeback are enforced in one place rather than per vCenter. Self-service is the whole point: it removes the platform team from the provisioning path while keeping them in control of the guardrails.
components.examTip: One VCF Automation instance per fleet, running in the first instance's management domain. Know that it is built on vSphere Supervisor and that provider versus organization portal is the governance split.

components.name: All Apps Organization
components.what: An organization is the top-level tenancy construct in VCF Automation, representing a tenant, business unit or line of business in a secure and isolated environment. There are two types. An All Apps organization is backed by vSphere Supervisor and vSphere namespaces and delivers the full built-in cloud services catalogue. A VM Apps organization is the transition path for existing Aria Automation users, is self-contained with its own cloud accounts, cloud zones and profiles, and runs virtual-machine-based applications only.
components.how: The provider administrator creates an All Apps organization, assigns it one or more Supervisors (or all available), sets zone-level CPU and memory limits and reservations, and selects the VM classes and storage classes it may use. Within the organization there is further isolation at project and namespace level, and quota assigned to the organization is subdivided into namespaces for project teams. Only one VM Apps organization can exist per VCF Automation instance; All Apps organizations can be many. All Apps requires a Supervisor with VPC networking to unlock the complete capability set.
components.why: Broadcom made All Apps the primary multi-tenancy model because it is the only one that delivers virtual machines and Kubernetes and data services through a single declarative platform with consistent quota, identity and isolation. VM Apps exists to protect existing Aria Automation investment during transition, not as a target state. Choose All Apps whenever the tenant needs both virtual machines and modern container workloads, which is the normal case for a development platform.
components.examTip: If the requirement mentions both virtual machines and Kubernetes or VKS, the answer is an All Apps organization. Remember only one VM Apps organization is permitted per VCF Automation instance, and that All Apps needs Supervisor with VPC.

components.name: vSphere Supervisor and Namespaces
components.what: vSphere Supervisor is a Kubernetes-based declarative control plane embedded into ESX, turning one or more vSphere clusters in a vCenter into an infrastructure-as-a-service platform. A vSphere namespace (also called a Supervisor namespace) is the logical boundary inside a Supervisor where workloads are deployed, carrying resource limits, permissions, networking and storage policies.
components.how: Supervisor can be enabled during workload domain creation or directly in vCenter, and a Supervisor is a collection of one or more clusters that can span multiple zones for fault tolerance. In the VCF Automation hierarchy, an organization contains projects, a project contains one or more namespaces, and a namespace is the envelope of resources in which virtual machines, VKS clusters and volumes are provisioned. Each namespace defines CPU, memory and storage limits, assigns available networks (a VPC, either dedicated or shared), assigns storage classes, and grants access to specific identity groups as owners. The Supervisor tracks desired state through custom resource definitions, so if a VKS worker node fails it detects the discrepancy and provisions a replacement automatically.
components.why: Broadcom made the namespace the fundamental building block because it is the only construct that simultaneously bounds compute quota, network isolation, storage class access and identity. That combination is what makes a namespace a genuine trust boundary rather than merely a folder, and it is why namespace layout is a security design decision rather than an organisational convenience.
components.examTip: Learn the hierarchy: organization, project, vSphere namespace, then workloads (VMs and VKS clusters). A namespace bounds quota, network, storage class and identity, which is why separate trust zones get separate namespaces.

components.name: VM Service
components.what: VM Service is the Supervisor capability that lets virtual machines be declared and managed as Kubernetes objects, using VM classes to define CPU and memory shape and content libraries to supply images. It is what makes traditional virtual machines first-class citizens of the same declarative API that serves containers.
components.how: A developer with access to a namespace creates a VirtualMachine resource specifying a VM class, an image and a storage class; the Supervisor provisions the virtual machine inside the namespace's quota, attaches it to the namespace's network (by default a private subnet in the namespace's VPC), and applies the namespace's storage policy. The provider controls what is possible by choosing which VM classes and storage classes each organization and namespace may use, so shape and service level remain governed even though provisioning is self-service. VM Service virtual machines can be placed on any of the VPC subnet types, though the default VM subnet set and interface are fixed.
components.why: Broadcom built VM Service so that platform teams do not have to run two parallel consumption models, one for virtual machines and one for containers. A single API, one quota model, one identity model and one storage policy framework covering both is a large manageability gain and it is what allows a development platform to serve legacy and modern applications from the same self-service catalogue.
components.examTip: VM Service plus VKS Service together is the answer when a requirement asks for self-service virtual machines and Kubernetes from the same platform. VM classes and storage classes are the provider's governance levers.

components.name: vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS)
components.what: VKS is the integrated service that provisions and lifecycle-manages upstream-conformant Kubernetes clusters as guest clusters on top of the Supervisor, deployed into a vSphere namespace. It is the successor naming for the Tanzu Kubernetes Grid service in the VCF lineage.
components.how: A consumer requests a cluster inside a namespace; the Supervisor provisions control plane and worker node virtual machines within the namespace's quota and network, and acts as the API control plane tracking cluster state through custom resource definitions. Node failure is detected and remediated automatically by reconciling desired state. Clusters get their networking from the namespace's VPC, with the NSX Container Plugin and load balancer integration providing subnets, IP address management, ClusterIP, LoadBalancer and Ingress service types and network policy. Because clusters are guest clusters, tenants get full cluster-admin rights inside their own cluster without any privilege on the underlying platform.
components.why: Broadcom offers VKS so that platform teams can deliver conformant Kubernetes as a service, with lifecycle handled by the platform, rather than having each application team build and operate its own clusters. The guest cluster model is what makes strong tenant isolation compatible with full cluster-admin freedom, which is precisely what a self-service development platform needs.
components.examTip: VKS clusters are guest clusters provisioned into a vSphere namespace with the Supervisor as control plane. In 9.1 a single Supervisor supports up to 500 clusters and Fast Deploy uses linked clones to accelerate provisioning.

components.name: Supervisor Zones
components.what: A Supervisor zone maps a Supervisor to vSphere cluster capacity for fault tolerance and placement. A Supervisor can span multiple zones, which allows workloads and Kubernetes control planes to be distributed across independent clusters, and a single Supervisor's resources can be mapped to multiple organizations through region quota.
components.how: Zones are laid out by mapping vSphere clusters to zones and then assigning zones with CPU and memory limits and reservations to organizations. The design decision is how many zones and what each one isolates: a single management zone for the platform's own consumption plane keeps its footprint and operations simple, while separate isolated zones per workload class or tenant give independent capacity and failure domains for the workloads themselves. Because VPCs are region-scoped, zone and region layout also constrains network mapping: namespaces in different regions necessarily use different VPCs.
components.why: Broadcom exposes zones so that a Supervisor's fault tolerance and capacity governance can follow the physical topology instead of ignoring it. Isolating workload zones from the management zone means a tenant workload cannot exhaust the capacity the consumption plane needs, and it keeps blast radius aligned with the cluster boundaries the infrastructure already has.
components.examTip: The recommended pattern is a single management zone plus isolated workload zones. Remember that a Supervisor can span zones for fault tolerance and that VPCs do not span regions.

keyFacts: A fleet has exactly one VCF Automation instance, running in the management domain of the first instance.
VCF Automation is built on the vSphere Supervisor platform.
Organization types are All Apps (Supervisor-backed, full cloud services catalogue) and VM Apps (self-contained, VM-only, transition path for Aria Automation users).
Only one VM Apps organization is permitted per VCF Automation instance; All Apps organizations can be many.
Hierarchy: organization, then project, then vSphere namespace, then workloads such as virtual machines and VKS clusters.
A vSphere namespace bounds CPU, memory and storage quota, assigned networks, storage classes and identity access, which is what makes it a trust boundary.
VPC networking on Supervisor is a prerequisite for the full All Apps capability set.
VM Service delivers virtual machines declaratively using VM classes and content library images; VKS Service delivers conformant Kubernetes guest clusters.
The provider governs what tenants can request through VM classes, storage classes, zone limits and reservations.
A Supervisor can span multiple zones for fault tolerance, and a single Supervisor can serve multiple organizations through region quota.
VPCs are region-scoped, so namespaces in different regions always map to different VPCs.
attentionItems: Choosing a VM Apps organization for a platform that needs Kubernetes. VM Apps runs VM-based applications only and is a transition construct.
Treating a namespace as an organisational folder. It is the boundary for quota, network, storage class and identity, so namespace layout is a security decision.
Placing multiple trust zones in one namespace and relying on naming conventions for separation.
Expecting the full All Apps capability set on VDS-backed or NSX classic networking. VPC is the prerequisite.
Forgetting that VCF Automation is a single fleet-level instance, so its availability and sizing are fleet-wide concerns tied to the management domain high availability decision.
Confusing the Supervisor with a VKS cluster. The Supervisor is the control plane and management construct; VKS clusters are guest clusters provisioned into namespaces.
Overlooking region and zone scoping when planning networks, since VPCs cannot span regions.
Assuming self-service means ungoverned. VM classes, storage classes, quotas and zone limits are the provider's control points and must be designed deliberately.

designDecisions.question: Should VCF Automation be deployed in a highly available configuration?
designDecisions.recommendation: Deploy VCF Automation in a highly available configuration consistent with the management components decision.
designDecisions.rationale: There is exactly one VCF Automation instance per fleet and it is the sole path through which tenants consume the platform. Its loss does not stop running workloads but it does stop all self-service provisioning, catalogue access and tenant operations across every organization in the fleet, which is a disproportionate impact for a single appliance failure on a platform whose primary purpose is self-service. Highly available deployment also aligns VCF Automation with the rest of the fleet-level services and, in 9.1, with the shared VCF services runtime on which it is hosted.
designDecisions.alternative: A single-instance deployment relying on vSphere HA to restart the appliance was rejected because it accepts a self-service outage on every host or appliance failure. It remains defensible where the customer explicitly accepts provisioning downtime and prefers the smaller footprint, which is why confidence is medium-high.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Availability of the consumption plane improves substantially. Manageability is mixed: fewer outages but more nodes, more certificate subject alternative names and additional sizing work. Recoverability improves through node redundancy and, in 9.1, unified backup of the shared runtime. Performance is neutral. Cost and management domain resource consumption increase.

designDecisions.question: Which VCF Automation organization type should the development platform use?
designDecisions.recommendation: Use an All Apps organization.
designDecisions.rationale: The development platform must deliver both virtual machines and Kubernetes clusters through self-service, and All Apps is the only organization type that does so: it is backed by vSphere Supervisor and vSphere namespaces and exposes the full built-in cloud services catalogue including virtual machines, Kubernetes, networking, volumes, registries, secrets and data services under one quota and identity model. It is also Broadcom's primary multi-tenancy model, so it is the supported target state.
designDecisions.alternative: A VM Apps organization was rejected because it runs VM-based applications only, cannot deliver VKS, and exists as a transition path for existing Aria Automation users rather than as a target architecture. Only one VM Apps organization is permitted per VCF Automation instance in any case.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Manageability improves substantially through one consumption model, one quota model and one identity model for virtual machines and containers. Security improves through organization, project and namespace isolation. Performance is neutral. The dependency created is a hard one: All Apps requires Supervisor with VPC networking, which ties this decision to DD-706.

designDecisions.question: How should vSphere namespaces be allocated across the development platform's workloads?
designDecisions.recommendation: Create a separate vSphere namespace for each trust boundary, rather than sharing namespaces across trust zones.
designDecisions.rationale: A namespace is the construct that simultaneously bounds compute and storage quota, assigned networks, storage class access and identity permissions. That makes it the platform's actual security boundary, so trust zones that must not reach each other's workloads, consume each other's quota or share identity grants belong in separate namespaces, each mapped to an appropriate VPC. Separate namespaces also make quota exhaustion and misconfiguration blast radius per-team rather than platform-wide.
designDecisions.alternative: A single shared namespace with naming conventions and labels for separation was rejected because conventions are not enforcement: quota, network reachability and role bindings would all be shared, so a single misconfiguration or a noisy team would affect every workload in the namespace.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Security improves materially through enforced isolation of network, quota and identity per trust zone. Availability improves because quota exhaustion is contained. Manageability is mixed: more namespaces to create and govern, offset in 9.1 by self-service namespace provisioning that inherits registry, ingress, quota and identity from existing VCF constructs. Performance is neutral, though VPC and subnet planning becomes more involved.

designDecisions.question: How hard should the tenancy boundary be between consumer groups?
designDecisions.recommendation: Implement hard logical tenancy using VCF Automation organizations, with projects and namespaces providing further isolation inside each organization.
designDecisions.rationale: Organizations are the top-level tenancy construct and give each tenant a secure and isolated environment in which they can see and consume only what has been allocated to them, with their own portal, identity mapping, quota and catalogue. That is a genuine logical boundary enforced by the platform rather than a naming convention, and it supports secure infrastructure isolation, quotas and chargeback. Projects and namespaces then subdivide the organization for individual teams.
designDecisions.alternative: Soft tenancy, using one organization with projects alone to separate consumer groups, was rejected because it puts every tenant in the same top-level boundary, sharing catalogue and organization-level administration. Physical tenancy, giving each tenant its own infrastructure, was rejected as disproportionate: it multiplies vCenter, NSX and hardware footprint for isolation that the organization construct already provides. Confidence is medium-high because the correct answer depends on the strength of the customer's separation requirement, and a genuinely regulated tenant may still justify physical separation.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Security improves through platform-enforced tenant isolation with per-tenant identity and quota. Manageability improves for tenants (their own portal and catalogue) and increases for the provider (more organizations to govern). Availability and performance are neutral, since tenants still share underlying capacity governed by zone limits and reservations. Cost is far lower than physical tenancy.

designDecisions.question: Which Supervisor services should be enabled to satisfy the self-service requirement?
designDecisions.recommendation: Enable both VM Service and VKS Service.
designDecisions.rationale: The platform must serve traditional virtual-machine applications and modern container workloads from one self-service interface. VM Service delivers virtual machines declaratively using provider-governed VM classes and content library images; VKS Service delivers conformant Kubernetes guest clusters whose lifecycle the Supervisor manages. Enabling both gives one API, one quota model, one identity model and one storage policy framework across both workload types, which is the manageability outcome the design is aiming for.
designDecisions.alternative: Enabling VKS Service only was rejected because it leaves virtual machine provisioning outside the self-service model, requiring a parallel process for the majority of existing workloads. Enabling VM Service only was rejected because it cannot deliver the Kubernetes capability the development platform requires.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Manageability improves substantially by collapsing two consumption models into one. Security is consistent because both workload types inherit namespace identity, network and storage policy. Performance is neutral, and in 9.1 Fast Deploy materially shortens provisioning time for both. Availability of provisioning depends on the Supervisor and on VCF Automation, linking back to DD-901.

designDecisions.question: How should Supervisor zones be laid out?
designDecisions.recommendation: Use a single management zone for the consumption plane plus isolated workload zones for tenant workloads.
designDecisions.rationale: Keeping the consumption plane in one management zone keeps its footprint and operational model simple, while isolating tenant workloads into their own zones means a tenant cannot exhaust the capacity the platform's own services need and gives each workload class an independent capacity and failure domain aligned to the underlying vSphere clusters. Because a Supervisor can span zones, this layout can also be used to give workloads fault tolerance across clusters.
designDecisions.alternative: A single zone shared by the management plane and all workloads was rejected because tenant capacity demand would then compete with the consumption plane and blast radius would span everything. A separate zone per tenant was rejected as disproportionate at this scale, since organizations, projects and namespaces already provide tenant isolation, and per-tenant zones would fragment capacity. Confidence is medium because the right number of zones depends on cluster topology and growth, which are still being validated.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Availability improves through capacity and failure isolation between the consumption plane and workloads. Manageability is mixed: clearer capacity governance, but more zones to map and more region quota to administer. Performance improves through contention isolation. A constraint to respect is that VPCs are region-scoped, so zone and region layout directly shapes network mapping.

vcf91Updates.title: VCF Automation 9.1 Fast Deploy
vcf91Updates.description: VKS and VM Fast-Deploy use linked clone technology to accelerate deployment and upgrade of VKS clusters and virtual machines, with linked clones of first class disks enabling fast provisioning of container storage volumes. Broadcom reports around 70 percent faster provisioning and around 75 percent shorter maintenance downtime windows, alongside support for up to 500 Kubernetes clusters per Supervisor.
vcf91Updates.impact: Provisioning-time service level objectives become far easier to satisfy, which directly affects the targets instrumented in DD-1003, and the higher per-Supervisor cluster ceiling means DD-906 zone layout is driven by isolation rather than by scale limits.

vcf91Updates.title: Container Service separation and simplified Container-as-a-Service
vcf91Updates.description: VCF 9.1 separates the container service concern from full Kubernetes cluster management, adding self-service namespace provisioning with registry, ingress, quotas and identity inherited from existing VCF constructs. This gives a simpler, faster path to running a small number of containers without operating a full Kubernetes cluster.
vcf91Updates.impact: There is now a lighter consumption tier between a virtual machine and a full VKS cluster, which changes how namespaces are offered to tenants under DD-903 and can reduce the number of full VKS clusters a development platform needs.

vcf91Updates.title: Infrastructure policies and delegated network security services
vcf91Updates.description: VCF Automation 9.1 adds tenant management improvements, self-service namespace provisioning with inherited VCF constructs, and infrastructure policies that delegate control of services such as vDefend firewall and Avi load balancing to organizations within provider-defined guardrails.
vcf91Updates.impact: The provider governance model in DD-904 becomes richer: more capability can be delegated to tenants without weakening the boundary, because policy rather than manual provider action defines what a tenant may configure.

vcf91Updates.title: Mixed organization models sharing vCenter and NSX
vcf91Updates.description: VCF Automation 9.1 allows the VM Apps and All Apps organization models to run simultaneously and to share the same vCenter and NSX infrastructure, removing the previous requirement to stand up separate vCenter and NSX environments to adopt the Supervisor-based model.
vcf91Updates.impact: Adopting All Apps under DD-902 no longer forces an all-at-once cutover for existing Aria Automation consumers, so a phased transition is possible without duplicating infrastructure.

title: Day 2 Operations
summary: Day 2 is where the design is proven or disproven in production. VCF Operations provides the instrumentation stack: policies set what is evaluated and at what thresholds, symptoms are the individual test conditions, alert definitions combine symptoms with recommendations and actions, notifications route alerts outward, and super metrics compute values the platform does not natively collect. Dashboards present the result. The design task is to instrument the service level objectives the business actually agreed to, using all of these capabilities together rather than a subset.

components.name: VCF Operations
components.what: VCF Operations is the fleet-level operations, observability and lifecycle console for VCF, the successor to Aria Operations. There is exactly one VCF Operations instance per fleet, running in the management domain of the first instance, and it also surfaces the centralised lifecycle and identity workflows and, in 9.1, the workflows previously in the SDDC Manager user interface.
components.how: It collects metrics, properties and events from adapters across vCenter, ESX, vSAN, NSX and the VCF management components, optionally through cloud proxies and collector groups for scale and availability. Collected data is evaluated against policies and alert definitions, presented through dashboards and views, and acted on through actions and notifications. In the high availability model it is a three-node cluster (primary, replica, data) with node size selected from the forecast virtual machine and object count across all connected instances. Because it is fleet-scoped it is the single place where estate-wide health, capacity, compliance and lifecycle state are visible.
components.why: Broadcom consolidated operations at the fleet level so that one console covers every instance and domain, which is what makes consistent service level measurement and capacity management possible across an estate. Making it also the lifecycle console in 9.1 removes the split between operating the platform and upgrading it.
components.examTip: One VCF Operations instance per fleet, in the first instance's management domain, three nodes in the high availability model. In 9.1 it is also where lifecycle work lives because the SDDC Manager user interface is deprecated.

components.name: Policies
components.what: A policy in VCF Operations is the container that determines how objects are analysed and monitored: which alert definitions and symptom definitions are active, what thresholds apply, how capacity and analysis settings behave, and which super metrics are calculated. Policies are assigned to object groups, and local policies can inherit from base policies or override them.
components.how: Each policy carries packages of alert definitions and symptom definitions that can be individually activated, deactivated or left to inherit, and for symptoms you can override threshold, criticality, wait cycles and cancel cycles. Wait and cancel cycles are the anti-noise mechanism: they require a condition to persist for several collection cycles before a symptom triggers and before it clears. A super metric must be enabled in the applicable policy before it is calculated, which is the single most common reason a newly created super metric appears to do nothing. Because policies are scoped to object groups, the same metric can carry a strict threshold on production objects and a relaxed one on development objects.
components.why: Broadcom uses policies so that monitoring behaviour is differentiated by service level rather than uniform across the estate. Without them, a threshold strict enough for production generates constant noise on a development platform, and operators learn to ignore alerts, which defeats the entire instrumentation exercise.
components.examTip: Policies control what is active and at what threshold, per object group, with inheritance from base policies. Remember that super metrics must be activated in the policy to be calculated.

components.name: Symptoms
components.what: A symptom definition is a single test condition evaluated against an object: a metric or super metric crossing a threshold, a property having a particular value, a message event, a fault event, or a metric event. Symptoms are the atoms of the alerting system and generate no notification on their own.
components.how: You define a symptom by choosing the object type, the metric or property or event, the comparison and threshold, and the criticality, then tuning wait cycles and cancel cycles to control sensitivity. Thresholds can be static or dynamic, where dynamic thresholds are learned from the object's own historical behaviour, which is useful for metrics with no universally correct fixed value. Symptoms can be created standalone or inline while building an alert definition, and they are activated or deactivated per policy.
components.why: Broadcom separates symptoms from alerts so that conditions are reusable and composable. A single symptom such as high memory utilisation can participate in several alert definitions with different companions, and an alert can require a combination of symptoms before firing, which is what allows alerting on a genuine problem signature rather than on one noisy metric.
components.examTip: Symptom equals one test condition. Symptoms do not notify; alerts do. Know the symptom source types (metric or super metric, property, message event, fault event, metric event) and that wait and cancel cycles control noise.

components.name: Alerts
components.what: An alert definition is a combination of symptoms plus recommendations, and optionally actions, which generates an alert when its symptom set becomes true. Alerts are classified against the Health, Risk or Efficiency badge and carry a criticality and an impact.
components.how: You build an alert definition by selecting the object type, adding one or more symptoms with the logic that combines them, choosing the badge and criticality, and attaching recommendations. Recommendations are the remediation guidance an operator sees and can be text instructions, links, or actual executable actions such as setting virtual machine memory. Notification rules then route generated alerts outward through outbound settings, for example to an email alias, an SNMP trap or a REST endpoint, with payload templates shaping the message. Alerts can be grouped for management, and log-based alert definitions can be created from log data as well as metrics.
components.why: Broadcom couples recommendations to alert definitions because an alert without a remediation path just transfers a problem to someone who does not know what to do about it. Attaching actions closes the loop further, allowing the response to be executed from the alert. Routing through notification rules keeps the decision about who is told separate from the decision about what constitutes a problem.
components.examTip: Alert definition equals symptoms plus recommendations, with optional actions. Notifications and outbound settings are what deliver the alert to an email alias or external system, which is the mechanism behind the phase 1 support alias requirement.

components.name: Key Performance Indicators
components.what: In an operations design, key performance indicators are the small set of measures that express whether the platform is meeting its service level objectives. They are drawn from collected metrics, from super metrics, or from timestamp-derived measures such as provisioning duration, and they are what dashboards and service level reporting present.
components.how: You derive key performance indicators from the non-functional requirements: if the requirement is a provisioning time target, the indicator is provisioning duration with percentile aggregation; if the requirement is capacity headroom, the indicator is remaining capacity and time remaining. For latency and duration measures, percentiles rather than averages are the correct aggregation, because an average hides the tail that users actually experience. Publishing the 95th and 99th percentiles alongside the failure count gives an honest picture, and setting a symptom on the indicator crossing its objective turns measurement into alerting.
components.why: Broadcom's operations guidance pushes towards a small curated indicator set because dashboards showing every available metric are unreadable and therefore unused. Restricting the indicator set to those tied to agreed objectives is what makes the operations layer a management tool rather than a telemetry dump.
components.examTip: For any duration or latency objective, capture timestamps and report percentiles (p95 and p99) plus failure counts, and alert when the objective threshold is breached. Averages are the wrong answer.

components.name: Super Metrics
components.what: A super metric is a user-defined metric computed by a formula over other metrics and properties, across one object or across a set of related objects. It is how you measure something the platform does not natively collect, such as a ratio, a rollup across a cluster, or a business-relevant composite.
components.how: You write the formula in the super metric editor, referencing metrics on the object or on related objects and using functions and aggregations, assign the super metric to the relevant object types, and then activate it in the applicable monitoring policy. Only after policy activation is it calculated and available for dashboards, views, symptoms and alerts. Because super metrics can be used as the metric source of a symptom, they are the bridge from a custom measurement to an alert, which is what makes service level objectives that the platform does not natively track alertable.
components.why: Broadcom provides super metrics because no vendor can anticipate every organisation's service level definition. Rather than forcing customers to export data into an external system to compute a composite, the calculation lives with the data and participates in the same policy, symptom, alert and dashboard machinery as native metrics.
components.examTip: Two examinable points: a super metric is a formula-derived custom metric, and it must be enabled in the policy before it is calculated. It can be the source of a symptom, which is how custom objectives become alertable.

components.name: Dashboards
components.what: A dashboard in VCF Operations is a configurable canvas of widgets presenting metrics, alerts, object relationships, topology and capacity information. A network operations centre dashboard is the specific pattern of a single curated view intended for continuous display to an operations team.
components.how: You build a dashboard from widgets bound to object scopes and metrics, including super metrics, and share it with the roles that need it. The design discipline for a network operations centre view is subtraction: include only the indicators tied to agreed service level objectives and the alerts that require action, so that an operator can assess platform state at a glance. Deeper investigation belongs in separate drill-down dashboards and views, not on the wall display. In 9.1 Broadcom also improved the built-in VCF health dashboards and added advanced vSAN and component diagnostics.
components.why: Broadcom supports custom dashboards because out-of-the-box views are built for exploration, not for operational monitoring at a glance. One curated dashboard is a manageability decision: it gives the operations team a single agreed source of truth, avoids the proliferation of near-duplicate views nobody maintains, and makes it obvious when an indicator is missing.
components.examTip: The recommended pattern is one custom dashboard carrying the essential key performance indicators, not many dashboards and not everything on one screen. Curation is the point.

keyFacts: One VCF Operations instance per fleet, in the management domain of the first instance; three nodes in the high availability model.

The instrumentation chain is: policy sets what is active and at what threshold, symptom is a single test condition, alert definition combines symptoms with recommendations and optional actions, notification rules route the alert outward.
Symptoms can be based on metrics, super metrics, properties, message events, fault events or metric events.
Wait cycles and cancel cycles control alert sensitivity and are the primary anti-noise mechanism.
Thresholds can be static or dynamic, where dynamic thresholds are learned from the object's own history.
A super metric must be activated in the applicable policy before it is calculated.
Super metrics can be the metric source for a symptom, which is how a custom objective becomes alertable.
Recommendations are attached to alert definitions and can include executable actions such as setting virtual machine memory.
