Notification rules plus outbound settings deliver alerts to destinations such as an email alias, SNMP or a REST endpoint; payload templates shape the content.
Phase 1 alerting in the case study routes to the support email alias, per constraint C03.
For duration and latency objectives, capture timestamps and report the 95th and 99th percentiles plus failure counts; averages hide the tail.
The recommended dashboard pattern is one curated network operations centre view carrying the essential indicators.
attentionItems: Confusing symptoms with alerts. A symptom is one test condition and notifies nobody; an alert definition combines symptoms and can notify and recommend.
Creating a super metric and never enabling it in the policy, then concluding it is broken.
Using averages for latency or duration objectives. The 95th and 99th percentiles are what reflect user experience.
Building many dashboards instead of one curated view, so nobody maintains any of them and the operations team has no agreed source of truth.
Applying one uniform policy to production and development objects, which guarantees either noise or blindness.
Setting thresholds without wait and cancel cycles, producing flapping alerts that get ignored.
Creating alert definitions with no recommendations, which passes an unactionable problem to the operator.
Assuming an alert definition notifies by itself. Notification rules and outbound settings are separate configuration.
Instrumenting only infrastructure metrics and never the service level objectives the business actually agreed.

designDecisions.question: How many dashboards should be created for day 2 operations, and what should they contain?
designDecisions.recommendation: Create one custom network operations centre dashboard containing the essential key performance indicators and actionable alerts, with separate drill-down views for investigation.
designDecisions.rationale: A single curated dashboard gives the operations team one agreed source of truth that can be assessed at a glance and kept current. Restricting it to indicators tied to agreed service level objectives and to alerts that require action is what keeps it readable; investigation depth belongs in drill-down dashboards and views rather than on the primary display. It also makes gaps obvious, because a missing objective has no tile.
designDecisions.alternative: Relying on the out-of-the-box dashboards alone was rejected because they are built for exploration rather than for at-a-glance operational monitoring against this customer's objectives. Building many role-specific dashboards was rejected because near-duplicate views drift, go unmaintained and destroy the notion of a single source of truth.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Manageability improves substantially through one maintained view and a clear operational focus. Availability improves indirectly because genuine problems are noticed faster and are not lost in noise. Performance and security are neutral. The ongoing obligation is dashboard hygiene as objectives change.

designDecisions.question: Which VCF Operations capabilities should be used to instrument the platform?
designDecisions.recommendation: Use all of the capabilities together: policies, symptoms, alert definitions with recommendations, notifications, key performance indicators, super metrics and dashboards.
designDecisions.rationale: The capabilities form a chain in which each link depends on the others, so adopting a subset leaves the instrumentation broken. Policies scope what is evaluated and at what threshold per object group; symptoms are the individual conditions; alert definitions compose symptoms and attach recommendations and actions; notification rules deliver the result; super metrics supply the measures the platform does not natively collect and can act as symptom sources; dashboards present the curated indicator set. Metrics without alerts are unread, alerts without policies are noise, and custom objectives without super metrics cannot be measured at all.
designDecisions.alternative: Using dashboards and native alerts only was rejected because service level objectives that the platform does not natively track would be unmeasurable, and default thresholds would generate noise on development objects. Using alerts without curated dashboards was rejected because there would be no at-a-glance view of platform state against objectives.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Manageability improves substantially because monitoring becomes deliberate and differentiated by service level rather than default and uniform. Availability and recoverability improve through earlier and better-targeted detection. Manageability also carries a real cost: policies, super metrics and alert definitions are configuration that must be built, tuned and maintained. Performance and security are neutral.

designDecisions.question: How should the deployment or provisioning service level objective be instrumented?
designDecisions.recommendation: Capture start and completion timestamps for every provisioning request, compute duration, report the 95th and 99th percentiles alongside the failure count, and raise an alert when the objective threshold is breached.
designDecisions.rationale: A provisioning time objective is a distribution, not a single number, so it must be measured as one. Timestamps give the raw duration; percentiles expose the tail that users actually experience, which an average conceals; the failure count matters because a fast failure is not a success. Implementing the measure as a super metric makes it available to symptoms, so the objective becomes alertable rather than merely reportable, and it then appears on the single network operations centre dashboard.
designDecisions.alternative: Reporting average provisioning time was rejected because averages hide the tail and can look healthy while a meaningful share of requests breach the objective. Reporting success and failure counts alone was rejected because they say nothing about whether the time objective is met. Monthly manual reporting was rejected because it cannot trigger a response.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Manageability and performance visibility improve markedly, giving an evidence base for capacity and tuning decisions. Availability improves indirectly through earlier detection of degradation. The cost is configuration effort: super metrics, symptoms, alert definitions and dashboard tiles to build and maintain. In 9.1, Fast Deploy substantially shortens provisioning times, so the objective threshold should be reviewed after upgrade.

vcf91Updates.title: Layered security patching with live patching
vcf91Updates.description: VCF 9.1 applies patches directly to running kernel memory on TPM-enabled ESX hosts, so virtual machines keep running with no maintenance window and no host evacuation, covering up to 80 percent of patches. Upgrade pre-checks evaluate system health and resource capacity before an upgrade runs, and parallel patching capacity rises to 256 clusters concurrently.
vcf91Updates.impact: Patching moves from a scheduled outage activity to a largely continuous one, which changes maintenance window planning, the capacity reserved for host evacuation, and the operational key performance indicators worth tracking, such as patch currency and time to patch.

vcf91Updates.title: Continuous compliance enforcement and configuration drift visibility
vcf91Updates.description: VCF 9.1 adds fleet-wide policy enforcement with granular visibility into configuration changes and drift across VCF instances, vCenter instances and individual clusters, including centralised enforcement of security settings such as password policy that previously had to be configured per component. Proactive diagnostics improve VCF health dashboards and add advanced vSAN and NSX component diagnostics.
vcf91Updates.impact: Compliance and drift become continuously measured platform states rather than periodic audit exercises, which adds compliance and drift indicators to the curated dashboard in DD-1001 and reduces the volume of custom instrumentation needed under DD-1002.

title: Migration
summary: Migration into the new workload domain is executed with HCX (VCF Operations HCX), which supplies several migration methods with different downtime, parallelism and scale characteristics: Cold, Bulk, vMotion, Replication Assisted vMotion (RAV) and OS Assisted Migration. The design work is matching method to workload tolerance, planning waves with dependency and rollback in mind, validating each wave before the next, and keeping the source environment intact as the fallback until acceptance.

components.name: HCX (VCF Operations HCX)
components.what: HCX is the workload mobility platform of VCF, providing interconnect, WAN optimisation, network extension and multiple migration technologies between two HCX-activated sites, or between clusters within a single vCenter. In the VCF 9 lineage it is branded VCF Operations HCX.
components.how: You pair the source and destination sites, define a compute profile at each end, and deploy a service mesh that instantiates the interconnect appliances, including the HCX-IX interconnect appliance whose mobility agent performs vMotion, Cold and RAV migrations, and optionally a Layer 2 network extension so that migrated workloads can retain their IP addresses. Migrations are then submitted as batches, each with a chosen method, and can be scheduled for a specific switchover window. HCX can also be used within a single vCenter when source and destination are different clusters, using the same compute profile and service mesh mechanics.
components.why: Broadcom provides HCX so that migration into a new platform does not require re-addressing workloads, rebuilding virtual machines or accepting long outages. Network extension in particular is what removes the need to co-ordinate an IP change with every application team, which is usually the largest source of migration risk and delay.
components.examTip: Know that the HCX-IX interconnect appliance's mobility agent performs vMotion, Cold and RAV migrations, that Layer 2 network extension lets workloads keep their addresses, and that HCX also works between clusters in a single vCenter.

components.name: Cold Migration
components.what: Cold migration moves a powered-off virtual machine using the VMware Network File Copy protocol. HCX selects it automatically when the source virtual machine is powered off.
components.how: The virtual machine's files are copied to the destination while it is off, then registered there. Because nothing is running, there is no memory or state transfer and no synchronisation phase, but the outage lasts for the whole copy, which makes duration a function of virtual machine size and available bandwidth. It suits workloads that are already off, decommissioning candidates, templates, and anything whose owner is happy to schedule a long window.
components.why: Cold migration exists as the simplest and lowest-risk method: with no running state there is nothing to keep in sync and little to go wrong. Broadcom keeps it in the toolkit because a meaningful share of any estate does not need to stay online, and spending live-migration capability on those workloads wastes both time and bandwidth.
components.examTip: Cold equals powered off, Network File Copy protocol, long downtime, small scale. It is selected automatically for powered-off virtual machines.

components.name: Bulk Migration
components.what: Bulk migration uses vSphere Replication (host-based replication) to move many virtual machines in parallel, with a switchover that interrupts service for roughly the duration of a reboot. It is the highest-scale HCX method.
components.how: Replication performs an initial full synchronisation to the destination while the source virtual machine keeps running, with duration determined by virtual machine size, data change rate and available bandwidth. Switchover can then start immediately or be deferred to a scheduled maintenance window. At switchover the source virtual machine is shut down, a final offline synchronisation completes, and the virtual machine is instantiated at the destination; the original is retained in a Migrated VMs folder, which gives a straightforward rollback. Bandwidth and network conditions must be sufficient for the switchover given the dataset and change rate.
components.why: Broadcom designed bulk migration for volume: it is the method that moves hundreds of workloads inside a window because it works in parallel and is resilient to interruption during replication. The reboot-equivalent interruption is the price of that parallelism, which is why it fits workloads whose owners can accept a short, scheduled restart.
components.examTip: Bulk equals parallel, largest scale, schedulable, interruption equivalent to a reboot. Choose it when a short cutover is acceptable. The retained copy in the Migrated VMs folder is the rollback path.

components.name: vMotion Migration
components.what: HCX vMotion uses the vMotion protocol to move a single running virtual machine's live state, including active memory, execution state, IP address and MAC address, to the remote site with no service interruption.
components.how: Memory pages are copied iteratively while the virtual machine keeps running, then execution switches to the destination in a window short enough to be transparent to applications and clients. Because it operates on one virtual machine at a time and is serial within a migration group, it does not scale to large batches. It requires sufficient bandwidth and low enough latency to complete the memory convergence.
components.why: Broadcom offers vMotion for the workloads where any interruption is unacceptable and the count is small: a handful of sensitive systems, or a pilot to prove the interconnect end to end before committing to a wave. Its serial nature is why it is not the answer for large-scale migration, however attractive its zero downtime is.
components.examTip: vMotion equals zero downtime but serial and one virtual machine at a time, so small scale. If a question pairs zero downtime with large scale, the answer is RAV, not vMotion.

components.name: Replication Assisted vMotion (RAV)
components.what: RAV combines the advantages of bulk migration (parallel operations, resiliency and scheduling) with those of vMotion (zero-downtime state migration). It requires the HCX Enterprise licence tier.
components.how: RAV replicates many virtual machines in parallel using replication, exactly as bulk migration does, and keeps them synchronised until the switchover window. At switchover it performs the final transition one virtual machine at a time using vMotion, transferring memory and execution state so each individual workload experiences no downtime. Because only deltas plus memory contents move at switchover, the switchover phase is short even though the initial replication can take longer than a small number of vMotions would. Switchover windows can be scheduled, and progress is tracked per virtual machine.
components.why: Broadcom built RAV precisely for the case the other methods cannot serve: a large migration where the workloads cannot take even a reboot. It resolves the historical trade-off between parallel scale and zero downtime, which is why it is the default recommendation for migrating a substantial estate of production-sensitive workloads.
components.examTip: RAV equals parallel replication plus zero-downtime switchover, larger scale, HCX Enterprise licence required. It is the answer for large-scale migration with minimal interruption.

components.name: Wave Planning, Validation and Rollback
components.what: Wave planning is the practice of grouping workloads into sequenced migration batches, each with a defined method, window, validation step and rollback path, instead of attempting a single cutover. Validation confirms each wave before the next begins, and rollback is the pre-agreed route back if validation fails.
components.how: Waves are grouped by application dependency, by downtime tolerance and by risk. The first wave is deliberately low-risk and serves to prove the interconnect, the network extension, the destination storage policy and the operational runbook end to end. Each wave then follows the same cycle: replicate, switch over in the agreed window, validate against explicit criteria (power state, guest health, application transaction, network reachability, backup coverage, monitoring visibility), and only then release the next wave. Rollback relies on the source environment remaining intact: bulk migration retains the original in a Migrated VMs folder, and keeping source hardware powered and licensed until acceptance is what makes reversal possible rather than theoretical. Method selection varies by wave, with cold migration for powered-off workloads, bulk where a short reboot is acceptable, and RAV where it is not.
components.why: Broadcom's migration guidance is wave-based because migration risk compounds: a problem discovered after everything has moved has no cheap remedy. Waves bound the blast radius of any single mistake, produce learning that improves later waves, and preserve a decision point at which the programme can stop. Validation is what makes the rollback decision evidence-based instead of a judgement call under pressure.
components.examTip: Expect scenario questions on sequencing and rollback. The correct pattern is a low-risk proving wave first, explicit validation criteria per wave, and the source environment retained as the fallback until formal acceptance.

keyFacts: HCX methods are Cold, Bulk, vMotion, Replication Assisted vMotion (RAV) and OS Assisted Migration; HCX Assisted vMotion (Direct) is also available.
Cold migration uses the Network File Copy protocol, is chosen automatically for powered-off virtual machines, and incurs downtime for the whole copy.
Bulk migration uses vSphere Replication, is parallel and schedulable, and its interruption is equivalent to a reboot.
vMotion migration has no service interruption but is serial, one virtual machine at a time, so it does not scale.
RAV combines bulk's parallelism, resiliency and scheduling with vMotion's zero-downtime state transfer, and requires HCX Enterprise.
RAV replicates in parallel and then switches over one virtual machine at a time with no downtime for each workload.
OS Assisted Migration handles guest (non-vSphere) workloads such as Hyper-V and KVM and involves conversion downtime.
The HCX-IX interconnect appliance's mobility agent performs vMotion, Cold and RAV migrations.
Layer 2 network extension lets migrated workloads retain their IP addresses, removing the need for co-ordinated re-addressing.
Bulk migration retains a copy of the original virtual machine in a Migrated VMs folder, which supports rollback.
Bulk and RAV both support scheduled switchover windows; vMotion and Cold do not schedule in the same way.
HCX can migrate between clusters within a single vCenter, not only between separate sites.
attentionItems: Choosing vMotion for a large migration. It delivers zero downtime but is serial, so it cannot meet the scale requirement; RAV is the method that does both.
Choosing bulk migration for workloads that cannot tolerate a restart. Bulk's interruption is reboot-equivalent by design.
Overlooking the HCX Enterprise licence dependency for RAV and OS Assisted Migration when RAV is the recommendation.

Sizing migration on virtual machine count alone. Replication duration depends on virtual machine size, data change rate and available bandwidth, and the switchover needs enough bandwidth for the final synchronisation.
Decommissioning or repurposing source hardware before formal acceptance, which destroys the rollback path.
Migrating without Layer 2 extension and without a re-addressing plan, then discovering every application team must co-ordinate an IP change.
Defining validation as 'the virtual machine powered on'. Validation should cover guest health, an application transaction, network reachability, backup coverage and monitoring visibility.
Starting with the most critical application. The first wave should be low risk and exist to prove the interconnect and the runbook.
Forgetting that migrated workloads land on a new storage policy and a new network model, so destination FTT policy and VPC or segment mapping must be settled before the first wave.

designDecisions.question: Which HCX migration method should be used for the bulk of the workload migration into the new workload domain?
designDecisions.recommendation: Use Replication Assisted vMotion (RAV) as the primary method, with bulk migration where a short reboot is acceptable and cold migration for workloads that are already powered off.
designDecisions.rationale: The migration is large and the workloads cannot generally absorb an outage, and RAV is the only method that satisfies both conditions: it replicates many virtual machines in parallel with resiliency and scheduled switchover windows, then performs each switchover one virtual machine at a time using vMotion so no individual workload experiences downtime. Because only deltas plus memory contents transfer at switchover, the cutover window stays short even for a large batch. Reserving bulk for reboot-tolerant workloads and cold for powered-off ones conserves RAV capacity and bandwidth for the workloads that actually need it.
designDecisions.alternative: Bulk migration alone was rejected as the primary method because its switchover interruption is reboot-equivalent, which the downtime-sensitive workloads cannot accept. vMotion alone was rejected because it is serial and one virtual machine at a time, so it cannot deliver the required scale within any realistic window. Cold migration alone was rejected because it requires the workload to be off for the entire copy.
designDecisions.amprsImpact: Availability during migration is preserved because individual workloads do not go down at switchover. Recoverability is supported by wave-based execution with the source environment retained as the fallback until acceptance. Manageability requires the HCX Enterprise licence tier, service mesh and interconnect configuration, and wave scheduling discipline. Performance depends on interconnect bandwidth and the workloads' data change rate, both of which must be measured before wave sizing, and the observed uplink utilisation makes bandwidth a live risk.

vcf91Updates.title: No major migration changes in VCF 9.1
vcf91Updates.description: VCF 9.1 introduces no significant changes to the HCX migration methods. Cold, Bulk, vMotion, Replication Assisted vMotion and OS Assisted Migration behave as in 9.0, and the component continues to be branded VCF Operations HCX.
vcf91Updates.impact: DD-1101 is unaffected by the 9.1 upgrade. Two adjacent 9.1 changes are worth noting during migration planning: VCF Import and the converge capability integrated into VCF Installer and VCF Operations offer an alternative to workload-by-workload migration where existing vSphere estates can be brought into VCF in place, and vVols deprecation means any source workloads on Virtual Volumes need a target storage model decided before their wave runs.
